alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A1:
SIMMONS APPEALS TO A MOB.
U. S. Senator Asks That a Negro Suspected of Killing His Father Be Spared.
RALEIGH, N. C., Sept. 14.—The Coroner's jury in Jones county to-night rendered a verdict that Farnifold G. Simmons, father of United States Senator Simmons, was murdered yesterday by "parties unknown." Circumstances point strongly to Alfred Daniels, a negro who has been arrested for the crime, who was seen in the woods the morning of the murder and had been heard to declare that he would either shoot squirrels on the plantation or would shoot old man Simmons.

Daniels is confined in the county jail at Trenton under double guard. Late this evening there was a large crowd of excited persons about the jail and there were threats of lynching. Senator Simmons appealed to the men to commit no act of violence, but to let the accused man have a fair trial.

The Sheriff said this afternoon that he did not believe an effort would be made to take the prisoner out of the hands of the law. Mr. Simmons was murdered on his plantation, near Pollocksville, Jones county, His body was found near a river. He had been shot and then clubbed to death. He was about 75 years old.
alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A2:
FOUL MURDER OF MR.F.G.SIMMONS
Father of United States Senator F. M. Simmons Shot by a Trespasser on His Land.
Alfred Daniels, now lies in Trenton jail, awaiting the verdict of the coroner's jury, which body is still in session. Mr. Simmons left his home on Saturday morning before breakfast with his gun for the purpose of killing game and stop treaspassers on his land. Shortly afterwards a report was heard, quickly followed by another but no attention was paid to them. Breakfast time came, Mr. Simmons did not return, search was made without results. Sunday a party of twenty-five men found the body near the Quaker Bridge road. Mr. Simmons had been shot. Eighteen No. 4 shot were found in his breast. He was fifty yards from his gun as if he had started crawling to the road. When shot he was sitting down.

The people of Craven county, once the home of Senator Simmons, are very much stirred up and mutters of lynching are often heard.

Mr. Taylor, the sheriff of Jones county, was in the city today. He said every precaution was taken to protect the negro in jail, a double guard is standing duty night and day. Senator F. M. Simmons is at the old homestead, where he was summoned by telegram Sunday.

The funeral service were held this afternoon, the remains were interred in the family burying ground. Rev. Mr. Rich, of New Bern officiated.

The news of the terrible tragedy was received in Raleigh with deep regret. At first it was not known how horrible this was.

The first intimation of it came in a telegram to Senator Simmons Saturday night, telling him that his father was missing from home. He was greatly troubled and alarmed and left on an early train Sunday morning for his father's home in Jones county.

On the way he learned that his father was dead and had been murdered. He sent back telegrams from New Bern informing his family of the shocking tragedy, and they left on the afternoon train for Jones county, going to New Bern from which they went by private conveyance to the home place.

Mr. Simmons leaves only a son, Senator F. M. Simmons, his wife having died a few years ago. It is said that until this death Senator Simmons was the only United States Senator whose father was living. In this sad hour the sympathy of the entire people of the State will go out to the deeply bereaved son and the stricken family.
alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A3:
MAY LYNCH NEGRO MURDERER.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]otte, N. C., Sept. 14.—Alfred Daniels.

[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

Charlotte, N. C., Sept. 14.—Alfred Daniels, the negro who murdered F. G. Simmons, father of United States Senator Simmons, has been captured, and is in jail. The negro had been working on Mr. Simmons's farm and accompanied him to Newbern when he sold $400 worth of cotton. Daniels shot Mr. Simmons in the stomach and then robbed him. The pistol and a large part of the money were found on the negro when he was arrested. He is now in jail at Trenton, and a lynching bee is not improbable. The Senator arrived at his father's house twelve hours after the body was found.
alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A5:
TAKEN TO NEW BERN
Alfred Daniels is Placed in the Jail There for Safe Keeping.
(Special to News and Observer.)

New Bern, Sept. 15.—Alfred Daniels, the negro to whom evidence points as the murderer of Mr. F. G. Simmons, the father of Senator Simmons, of Jones county, was brought to New Bern this morning by Sheriff Taylor, of Trenton, and lodged in Craven county jail for safe keeping until the next term of the criminal court.

I was told today if he had been left in Trenton jail last night he would have been lynched in spite of Senator Simmons and the ministers of Jones county pleading with them not to be guilty of the awful deed. Sentiment is still at its height against Alfred Daniels, but there is no fear of harm to him while in Craven county jail.

The coroner's jury rendered a verdict last night that Mr. Simmons came to his death by gunshot wounds from a gun in the hands of Alfred Daniels. The telephone message received here from Trenton as to the verdict was erroneous.

The remains of the deceased were interred in the family burying ground yesterday afternoon. The funeral services were conducted in the home by Rev. W. H Rich, pastor of the First Baptist church, of New Bern. A large concourse of friends were present from all parts of Jones and adjoining counties.

Mrs. F. M. Simmons, Mr. and Mrs. L. A. Mahler and Miss Eliza Simmons were there from Raleigh.

The pall-bearers were: John C. Parker, M. N. Harriett, John Pearce, F. H. Foy, C. J. DeBruhl, T. D. Warren, Thos. C. Whitaker and John W. Wooten.
alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A6:
Sen. Simmons Discourages Lynching
(Special to News and Observer.)
Trenton, N. C., Sept. 14.—The people of Jones county are terribly stirred up and aroused over the assassination of Mr. Simmons, and there are reports here that parties have talked of lynching the murderer if he can be located.

Senator Simmons, who is in Jones county, having reached here on Sunday morning, has discouraged any such purpose. He has urged the people to let the law vindicate itself and not to attempt to take the matter in their own hands.

Ever since the report of the murder the people have been gathering about the home of Mr. Simmons and during the day the crowd increased greatly. Whenever there was talk of lynching, Senator Simmons, as soon as he would hear of it, would personally ask that no such step be taken. The sheriff and others say that there will be no lynching.

It is reported today that there is another negro under suspicion and it is thought that he was either with Daniels, or that Daniels afterwards talked with him and asked his aid in secreting the body. This negro is said to be Dump King and the officers are searching for him.
alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A7:
A LESSON IN RESTRAINT.
There has not been a stronger lesson of respect to law and order than that which has just been presented to the State and the nation in the events about the murder of Mr. F. G. Simmons, the father of Senator Simmons.

Because of the relationship which existed between these two men the lesson is a more pointed one, and this will be emphasized in the eyes of the world because that the son is a United States Senator, representing North Carolina, and the State chairman of the Democratic party.

The negro at whom the circumstantial evidence pointed as the murderer of his father had been caught. The son, his heart over-flowing with deep grief, mind distracted because of the horrible death which had come to his venerable parent yet finds time to come from the house of mourning and to personally urge upon his neighbors, his friends and the people gathered, that they let the law take its course, and that there be no lynching.

There had been talk of this, and it had reached the ears of Senator Simmons. The people were deeply indignant at the brutal assassination and their feelings were aroused to that point that a quick end to the life of the murderer was thought of. At this juncture it was the words of an only son that saved the wretch's life, for it is said that but for the presence and pleas of Senator Simmons this would have been put an end to. It is a lseson in restraint that is not often taught so plainly and clearly. It is a lesson that should be taken to heart and considered when the fever of lynching possesses a people.
alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A11:
SAVED BY SENATOR SIMMONS.
Allusion was made in these columns at the time of the spirit of devotion to law that characterized the conduct of Senator Simmons upon the occasion of the awful and unprovoked assassination of his honored and aged father. The Senator would not countenance any suggestion of lynching the man guilty of the death of his father. In Monday's Washington Post, Mr. Claude N. Bennett cites the action of Senator Simmons as a notable instance of the triumph of law and order in North Carolina, and writes as follows:

"Here is an instance well worth your while of the triumph of law and order in the South:

"Some days ago a blameless white citizen of North Carolina was murdered by a negro. He was an old man of seventy-four—kind, law-abiding, and loved by his neighbors. He was the father of United States Senator F. M. Simmons. The negro was trespassing on Mr. Simmons' plantation. He had been previously warned—he persisted in the trespass. The old gentleman saw him, approached him, and ordered him away. The remonstrance was met with a club. The venerable man sank to his death. The negro laughed at his deed, threw his bloody club in the bushes, and went his way.

"Mr. Simmons was missed. His son, the Senator, who was in Raleigh, hastened to the old home in response to a telegram, and instituted search for his father. In two days the body was found. Shortly after the murderer was caught. He was clearly identified; his guilt was undenied. The mob was there—the passionate, lawless, uncontrolled and uncontrollable Southern mob. A Winchester was accessible to every man of them. Many of them had revolvers. All of them had knives. Rope was plentiful. Tar, pitch and turpentine are not scarce in North Carolina, and fire burns easily.

"The brute stood in their midst—sullen, dogged, unrepentant. Black of color, thick of lip, low of brow, full of hate, expecting no mercy. Senator Simmons had been several times chairman of the State Democratic committee. Under his leadership the State had been not long ago saved from the threatened negro control. Gratitude to him was in every heart. The Wilmington outrages, the red-shirt campaign, the late necessity of dealing with the negro question in heroic fashion were fiesh in every memory.

"Is it less than a modern miracle that this mob was dispersed and this negro taken peaceably to jail to await trial in regular process of law? The miracle was wrought by Senator Simmons—the most injured member of that party. He is a hot-blooded man. In discussing the negro question in the United States Senate he has been accused of intemperate speech. But the severest test was now upon him, and he met it like a Spartan judge. He stood up before that infuriate crowd and implored them to let the law take its course. He said he had no need to dwell upon his love for his father and grief at his remorseless taking off. That father had gone to his reward. The foul crime that sent him thence could not be wiped out or mitigated by further violation of law. To jail with the criminal—let the proud escutcheon of North Carolina be untarnished.

"Take this incident for what it is worth. But remember, in passing, that if this negro had committed the offense usually provocative of lynching in the South, forty thousand Senators and all the courts in Christendom could not have taken him to jail through that North Carolina mob."
alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A12:
GOES TO HIS TRIAL
Negro Charged With Murder of Sen. Simmons' Father Sent to Trenton.
(Special to News and Observer.)

New Bern, N. C., Nov. 2.—Alfred Daniels, the negro who is charged with the murder of Furman G. Simmons, father of Senator Simmons, was taken from Craven county jail Sunday night by Sheriff Taylor, of Jones county, and taken to Trenton, where he will be tried for the cruel and dastardly murder of one of the State's oldest and highly respected citizens.

Daniels was placed in Craven jail for safe keeping, as it was deemed unsafe to let him stay in Trenton, owing to the strong sentiment that was against him. All indications pointed to his guilt at the finding of Mr. Simmon's and it is said on good authority that the alleged murderer made a verbal confession to Sheriff Taylor, of Jones and Biddle of Craven that he killed Mr. Simmons in self-defense. Mr. Simpson's was found by his side with both barrels cocked but from the statement by the prisoner it was impossible for him to have shot Simmons from the position and location that he said he was in. The case will come up before Judge Henry H. Bryon R. Bryan, who is predicting at the criminal term of court.

alfred-daniels-trenton-1903-09-14.A22:
Daniels Put to Death.
Newbern, Special.—Alfred Daniels, the murderer of E. G. Simmons, father of United States Senator F. M. Simmons, was hanged at Trenton, at 1:38 p. m. The execution was without any special incident. Daniels displayed great nerve, and said that he was unjustly tried. He maintained that he was innocent of intentional murder, claiming he shot Mr. Simmons in self-defense. He professed religion and was baptised. There was a large crowd in town, but the hanging was private, being witnessed by only those who had tickets.

alvah-h-martin-berkley-1903-12-08.A1:
MOBBED BY DEMOCRATS
REPUBLICANS KICKED, CHOKED AND BEATEN AT NORFOLK, VA.
Assaulted by 300 Whites, Who Were Armed with Shotguns, Repeating Rifles, Revolvers and Clubs.
NORFOLK, Dec. 8.—Summoned by the ringing of the bell of the Berkeley-avenue Baptist Church to-night a mob of 300 white Democrats stormed the office of the Berkeley Baptist Church to-night a mob of 300 white Democrats stormed the office of the Berkeley Improvement Board, in which were County Treasurer Lyons, Commissioner of Revenue Nichols, Town Recorder Old, Deputy County Clerk W. H. Lyons and nearly a score of negroes, and rushed the entire party from the building to the street. County Treasurer Lyons was kicked half way down the stairs.

The crowd then assailed the Berkeley police station and found there County Clerk A. H. Martin, a Republican, seated at a table with Rev. John Sumler, a negro councilman. Martin was attacked, severely choked and slammed against a cell door. As he stood there, powerless, denunciatory speeches were delivered to him and he was then escorted to his home by the police.

The mob was composed of 300 men, all white, and nearly all armed, shotguns and repeating rifles being plentiful, while revolvers and clubs were also in evidence. Several shots were fired in the street, but no one was hurt.

The riot was caused by bitter political feeling which has existed between the straight-out Democratic element in Norfolk county and the fusion element controlled by Martin. It is charged by the Democrats that the county officials present in the office of the improvement board had assembled there to collect the poll taxes from negroes surreptitiously and that on the other hand obstacles are placed in the way of white Democrats qualifying to vote. In the crowd was C. W. Rockefeller, a first cousin of the Standard Oil magnate, and the Rev. Herbert Scholz, a Christian minister.
alvah-h-martin-berkley-1903-12-08.A3:
CAMPAIGN OPENS IN VIRGINIA Democrats Run Officer Out of Office Because He Registered Negro Voters. NORFOLK, Va., Dec. 8.—Democrats in the town of Berkley have driven County Treasurer Lyons from his office, where, it it charged, he was registering negro voters and had the negroes penned up in one section of the town. The streets are filled with men armed with shotguns, and a request will be made for a company of military from Norfolk or Portsmouth at once. Serious trouble is feared. ADVERSE TO SOLDIERS' HEIRS Department Holds That Widows and Orphans Must Live on Homesteads. REVERSES FORMER DECISION IN MATTER Decision is Made in Case of Mrs. Anna Bowles, Who Made Entry in the Broken Bow District.
WASHINGTON, Dec. 8.—To nullify attempts of cattle companies and others to obtain public lands in violation of the law the secretary of the interior today overruled former decisions of the department to the effect that widows or minor orphans of soldiers or sailors do not have to reside on the land on which they make homestead entry. The decision, which affects a large number of cases and which has an important hearing on the public land frauds, is made in the case of Mrs. Anna Bowles, who made an entry on land in the Broken Bow district in Nebraska. Mrs. Bowles claimed the right of entry as the widow of a sailor in the civil war, under a section of the revised statutes, which allows such dependents to make homestead entries with credit for the time of the soldier's or sailor's military or naval service. It was admitted in this case that she made an agreement with the Standard Cattle company, whereby Mrs. Bowles, at the time of the entry, leased the land to the company with further agreement that the company should have the option of purchase for the land. The department decides that Mrs. Bowles is required to maintain residence on the land and her agreement with the company invalidated the entry and requires its cancellation.

Briefs in Merger Case.

Briefs in behalf of the Northern Securities company and the Northern Pacific Railway company, in the case of the United States against those two companies and the Great Northern company, were filed in the supreme court today. The brief of the securities company is by George B. Young and that of the Northern Pacific by C. W. Bunn. Mr. Young's brief is a document of over 300 pages and in it he traces minutely the origin of the merger. Mr. Young contended that such a hodling as that of the Union Pacific in the Northern Pacific was not contrary to the anti-trust law and the "inaction of the attorney general showed that this also was the opinion of that high official, charged with the enforcement of the anti-trust act."

The brief of Mr. Bunn is an argument to show that the action of the two railroad companies did not come within the anti-trust act.

"This case is of local interest because the appellant, Mrs. Anna Bowles, is a resident of Omaha," said Attorney J. C. Kinsler last evening, who was Mrs. Bowles' counsel at Broken Bow and on September 3 last argued the case at Washington on the appeal taken from the decision of the commissioner of the general land office affirming that of the register at Broken Bow, that widows of sailors and soldiers must conform to the law of 1862 in making homestead entries, "and of national interest because thousands of widows and orphans will be affected by this decision.

"My client was required to make aid/davit conforming with the law of 1862, which law contemplates that all persons making homestead entries shall reside on the land so entered, and no doubt this decision is based on that promise," continued the attorney. "The third section of the law of 1872, passed and enacted by congress to reward the soldiers and sailors, confers the rights of the husband on the widow or guardian of minor children, if deceased. This decision indicates the Department of the Interior has gone back on the law of 1872. In my brief submitted in the case just decided, according to your dispatch, adversely to Mrs. Bowles I cited the law of 1872, which does not require a widow or guardian child to reside on the land. This decision affects twenty-two cases in all, which were instituted by me in the land office at Broken Bow."
alvah-h-martin-berkley-1903-12-08.A5:
MOB DRIVES OFF NEGROES. Wouldn't Allow Them to Pay Poll Taxes, a Preliminary to Voting.
NORFOLK, Va., Dec. 8.—A mob of straight-out Democrats drove the Fusionists and negroes from the poll tax office to-day. Alvah H. Martin, leader of the Fusionists, was thrown to the ground and seriously hurt. No one else was hurt by the mob, but many of the mob were injured. Many guns were fired for intimidation.

Under the new law every voter must pay his poll tax before he is qualified to vote and the offices are in the hands of the fusion faction of Democrats. They have made a ruling that everybody in Berkley should appear in the clerk's office in Portsmouth to pay his taxes. But this afternoon it was learned that the poll taxes of the fusionists, consisting chiefly of negroes, would be allowed to be paid at the office of George Martin in Berkley.

Treasurer Lyons was there to receive the taxes and a crowd of negroes was there to pay them. This incensed the straight-out factionists. They said they had been deceived.
alvah-h-martin-berkley-1903-12-08.A6:
PARTY RIOT IN BERKLEY
County Officers Alleged to Have Been Receiving Poll Taxes of Negroes Driven From the Building by Irate Democrats—Feeling Intense and Further Trouble Is Feared.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
NORFOLK, VA. Dec 8. The trou

(Npecial to The Times-Dispatch.)

NORFOLK, VA., Dec. 8.-The trouble that has been brewing between the county treasurer and the members of the Straightout faction in Norfolk county, who would have been disfranchised by not being assessed for poll-taxes, came to a head to-night in Berkley.

Treasurer Samuel W. Lyons was attending a meeting in Berkley, and the Straightouts believing he was receiving taxes for other parties, than they themselves, waited on him in force. They rang church bells to summon their friends, and appeared outside the Martin building, where the treasurer was engaged, armed and ready for anything. The crowd learned that negroes were being allowed surreptitiously to pay their poll-taxes, and this incensed the Straightout voters of Berkley, who claimed to have been prevented from paying their taxes by political dodges.

Assaulted Lyons.

They sought out Lyons at the Martin building, and assaulted and kicked him. It is claimed that he was found with a dozen negroes, Commissioner of the Revenue Nichols and other county officers. After cleaning out his office the crowd made-for the police station, where County Clerk A. H. Martin, leader of the Fusionists, was in conference with the Rev. J. Sumler, a colored Councilman.

The crowd broke through the police, who sought to stay their progress, and attacked Mr. Martin. They smashed his hat and choked him. Three of them, Clarence McCoy, W. H. Groves and R. Mcore, lectured the official while he was propped against a cell door. Many guns were exhibited in the police station, and at one time it was feared that murder might be done. Finally the police succeeded in restoring order, and the place was cleared. A number of warrants have been issued for those concerned in the attack on the station-house.

Further Trouble Feared.

Afterwards the crowd marched about the streets of Berkley or remained near the residence of Mr. Martin. Among them were many of the most prominent members of the Straightout party, including some of its candidates for the Legislature and for high county offices in the late campaign.

Feeling runs high between the two factions over the disfranchisement of voters not assessed, and further trouble is feared. Chairman G. W. Jones, of the Straightouts, was asked to-night if he had any statement to make in connection with the occurrence, and he declared that he had not.
alvah-h-martin-berkley-1903-12-08.A8:
SHOT-GUN POLITICS
No Arrests Made Yet of the Straightouts Who Attacked the Fusionists.
THEY JUSTIFY THEIR ACTION
Oportunities Alleged Given Negroes While Difficulties Were Thrown in Way White Men.
(Npecial to The Times-Dispatch.)

NORFOLK, VA., Dec. 0.—No arrests have as yet been made in connection with the riot of last night in Berkley, when the Straightouts went with shotguns to prevent the county treasurer from receiving the poll taxes of negro voters. The Straightouts defend their course by stating that the people had become exasperated by the obstacles persistently placed in the way of the white voter paying his poll taxes, while the negroes were reported to have everything made easy for them. This the fusionists deny. That there was no floodshed is considered remarkable. Feeling has now subsided, and there is no immediate prospect of further trouble. The city of Portsmouth will ask the legislature for permission to purchase the present water works system, which also supplies Suffolk and Berkley. Nearly two millions is involved in the transaction.

MOCCASIN NOT FLOATED.

All efforts to float the submarine torpedo boat Moccasin, which is still ashore on the beach at Currituck, have proved utile. The Merritt wrecking steamer rescue, while pulling on the Moccasin o-day, snapped a hawser and operations had to be temporarily suspended. It is believed that the little boat will be gotten off during the storm now preailing.

The shipping is hugging port to-night. There is a fierce storm off the Virginia coast, and although there have been no reports of disasters at sea, shipping masters are uneasy. All north-bound shipping out, as long as a day is imperilled by to-night's blow along the Middle Atlantic seaboard.

VACANCY ON BENCH.

Governor Montague will have to appoint a judge of the County Court of Princess Anne to fill out Judge B. D. White's term. The judge will retire from the bench to become Commonwealth's attorney some weeks before his term ends.

Six starving Portuguese, who came here from the Cape de Verde Islands, tempted by stories of fine wages, are being cared for at the Union Mission. When they arrived here they found that they would have to subsist on $10 a month, and they are now in pitiable distress. The Mayor will care for them temporarily.
alvah-h-martin-berkley-1903-12-08.A12:
BLOODY FIGHT SEEMS INEVITABLE.
Negro Voting Arouses Fierce Antagonism in Norfolk County, Va.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

Norfolk, Va., Dec. 11. A bloody clash appears inevitable between the straightout Democrats of Norfolk County and the Fusionists, composed of Democrats, Republicans and negroes. The whites say that they were denied the right to be assessed, while the negroes were surreptitiously allowed to pay the tax to vote next year. County Treasurer Lyons, one of the officials attacked on Tuesday night, announces that he will close his office to-morrow, the last day for paying the tax, at 5 p. m. It is known that this will be resisted by the straightouts. The fusionists are reported to be arming. The police force of Portsmouth, the county seat, is small.

At a massmeeting of the best citizens of Berkley, among them ministers, a redhot resolution was adopted, the most significant part of which is:

We are forced to declare to these people (fusionists) that we will no longer endure such conditions, and that singly and collectively we pledge our fortunes, our lives and our honor to use every honorable means known to free American citizens to overthrow this lawlessness that cloaks under the guise of law.
alvah-h-martin-berkley-1903-12-08.A15:
TROUBLE AT BERKLEY.
The Democrats of Berkley or rather certain lawless elements of that party went to the office of the county treasurer and drove away the colored men who were there to pay the poll taxes as a prerequisite to voting. These lawless elements were armed with shot-guns and threatened to use them. The County Treasurer was forced to seek an asylum in the station house. The reasons given were that this white treasurer received the poll-tax from colored men while difficulties were thrown in the way of white men. No arrests have been made as a result of this high-handed proceeding. It is rather surprising that the colored people in that section subnitted to it. They are as a rule property owners, thrifty and responsible and some of our best friends are to be found in that locality. benjamin-gorman-americus-1903-05-29.A1:
TO SLAYER OF KENT NO MERCY IS GIVEN
Murderer Was Lynched Near Preston.
YOUNG KENT WAS WELL KNOWN
Enraged Friends of the Young Man Capture Ben Gorman and String Him Up—Killing of Mr. Kent is Very Greatly Deplored,
Ben Gorman, the negro who brutally murdered Mr. Shelly Kent, a well known young farmer residing near Church Hill, in Webster county, has already paid the penalty of his crime at a rope's end, justice thus having been dealt him Friday evening.

News of the lynching of Gorman reached Americus yesterday.

The crime was one of the most atrocious ever committed in this section of the state, and the friends of the murdered man were not slow in wreaking vengeance upon his slayer.

The Times Recorder yesterday gave brief particulars of the killing of Mr. Kent, an estimable and highly respected citizen of Webster, though there were some errors in the published account of the tragedy. Mr. Kent was 21 years of age and held in highest esteem.

Mr. Kent and the negro, Gorman, were in the field together when, after a few words regarding some transaction between them, and while Mr. Kent's back was turned, Gorman dealt him a fearful blow upon the head with a hoe, crushing his shull.

Mr. Kent died a few hours thereafter, while Gorman fled.

Friday evening a number of the friends of the murdered man went in pursuit of Gorman and quickly effected his capture. The murderer was promptly lynched, and as far as his miserable life was concerned the murder of a good man was avenged.

The lynching was quietly conducted and no disorder ensued.
benjamin-gorman-americus-1903-05-29.A2:
NEGRO WAS LYNCHED FOR COMMITTING MURDER.
Americus, Ga., May 30.—Information reached Americus this afternoon of the capture and lynching yesterday evening of Benjamin Gorman, colored, for the murder of Shelley Kent, a prominent and highly respected young farmer residing near Church Hill, in Webster county.

The murder occurred Thursday, when Mr. Kent and Gorman were in a field at work, and was without provocation. After having some words with the negro, Kent turned to leave the field, when Gorman dealt him a fearful blow from behind, landing upon the head and crushing the skull.

Kent lingered some time, and after his death yesterday, enraged citizens captured Gorman and lynched him. Mr. Kent was highly respected and his tragic death greatly deplored.

Americus, Ga., May 30.—Information reached Americus today of the capture and lynching yesterday evening of Benjamin Gorman, colored, for the murder of Shelly Kent, a young farmer residing near Church Hill, in Webster county. The murder occurred Thursday when Kent and Gorman were in the field at work and was without provocation.
benjamin-gorman-americus-1903-05-29.A11:
FIFTEEN CENTS CAUSE MURDER AND LYNCHING
SKULL OF SHELLEY KENT, A YOUNG FARMER, CRUSHED WITH A HOE.
The Murderer Is Caught and Strung up by Enraged Citizens.—Kent Had Turned to Leave When He Was Killed.
Judge Lynch had a session of his court in Webster county Friday evening, the victim being a negro by the name of Ben Gorman, who the day before killed Shelley Kent, a well-known young white farmer of the Church Hill community.

The killing of Kent and the lynching of Gorman grew out of the small sum of fifteen cents which the latter owed the former, and the tragedy occurred in a field where the two were at work. After having some words with the negro Kent turned to leave the field, when Gorman dealt him a fearful blow from behind with a hoe, which landed upon the head and crushed the skull.

Kent lingered until Friday, and after his death enraged citizens lynched Gorman.

The negro, after his capture, was in the hands of Bailiff Marshall, who was endeavoring to take him to jail.

The crowd, while orderly, was determined to Lynch him, and after getting him from the hands of the officer very quickly strung him up to a tree.

SHOT FROM AMBUSH BY DISCHARGED NEGRO
(BY Associated Press.)
TOW. FLA. Dec. 24.—Colong

(By Associated Press.)
BARTOW, FLA., Dec. 24.—Colonel John Beaty, general manager of the Greenbay 1hosphate Company, while driving to his mines this morning, was shot from ambush by a negro, whom he had discharged yesterday. Mrs. Beaty was with him and was seriously hurt, several shots striking her about the face and breast. Colonel Beaty was not hurt very badly. Colonel Beaty's horse came near running away and the negro escaped in the woods. Posses have been scouring the woods all the day and late this afternoon a negro was captured who is supposed to be the right man. berry-henry-bartow-1903-12-24.A2:
SHERIFF OF NERVE
He Defies and Threatens Mob and Saves His Prisoner.
(By the Associated Press.)

Bartow, Fla., Dec. 26.—Night before last, shortly after dark, about twenty-five or thirty men, armed to the teeth, marched into this city and for a time it was thought that the crowd would make a determined effort to get Berry Henry, the negro who is in jail, supposed to be the one wanted for shooting Colonel and Mrs. John Beatty Thursday morning. But for the dogged determination of Sheriff Tilly, it is more than likely that they would have made a raid on the jail. With guns pointed at the officers they told him to get out of the way and let them have the negro; but he very coolly told them that if they advanced closer they would do so at their own peril.

The mob finally dispersed, being assured that the negro would be taken before Colonel Beatty for identification at the earliest possible moment. Henry was spirited to Tampa last night, the sheriff fearing another attempt to lynch him. Officers drove to Pridgen with the negro, where they boarded a train for Tampa.

Mrs. Beatty is not considered out of danger. The attending physician reports that her skull was fractured in one place. It is not at all certain that she will recover. Colonel Beatty's wound was slight.
berry-henry-bartow-1903-12-24.A3:
WANTED TO LYNCH
SHERIFFF'S PRISONER.
The Coolness of Tillis, However, Thwarted the Mob at Bartow

The Coolness of Tillis, However, Thwarted the Mob at Bartow

Bartow, Fla., Dec. 26.—Thursday night, shortly after dark, about twenty-five or thirty armed men marched into this city, and for a time it was thought they would make a determined effort to get Berry Henry, the negro who is in jail, supposed to be the one wanted for shooting Col. and Mrs. John Beaty Thursday morning. But for the coolness and the dogged determination of Polk county's sheriff, J. D. Tillis, it is more than likely that they would have made a raid on the jail. With guns almost pointed in the officer's face, they told him to get out of the way and let them have the negro; but he very coolly told them that if they advanced a little closer they would do so at their peril. The mob finally dispersed, being assured that the negro would be taken before Col. Beaty for identification at the earliest possible moment. There is pretty strong circumstantial evidence against the negro. His gun is a ten-bore, and some of the shells found in his possession carry the same size shot as that fired at Col. Beaty and wife. City Marshal Childs went to the place where the shooting occurred, and picked up from among the palmetto bushes pieces of the wadding used in the gun with which the almost fatal shooting was done, and it fits exactly with the wadding found in the shells in Henry's possession. His foot is the same size as the track leading directly from the place of the shooting to his home. Henry was spirited to Tampa last night. The sheriff, fearing another attempt to lynch him. Officers drove to Pridgen with the negro, where they boarded the train for Tampa.

biltmore-biltmore-1903-08-24.A2:
NEGROES BLANKET-TOSSED.
Skylarking Soldiers at Biltmore Carry Fun to the Trouble-Making Point.
RALEIGH, N. C., Aug. 25.—The village green at Biltmore, George W. Vanderbilts model village near Asheville, was the scene of a blanket bouncing last evening, when several negroes were handled roughly by soldiers belonging to the First Regiment, N. C. N. G. The regiment has been encamped at Biltmore for ten days and had just had its final drill and parade in the presence of Gov. Aycock and several thousand citizens of Asheville.

When the regiment had been reviewed by Gov. Aycock some soldiers decreed that no negroes should be allowed to remain in the neighborhood. The resolution was formed in a spirit of fun largely, but when several negroes, old and young, had been tossed up trouble began.

Several negroes were chased off the yards of the Southern Railway until one man, a negro brakeman, drew a revolver and threatened to shoot a soldier. He was arrested, but a representative of the Southern Railway Company took a hand in the matter and secured the negro's release on bail. It was said to-night that an old and infirm negro was handled roughly by some of the soldiers and that they threatened to throw another into the Swannanoa River. This negro escaped by saying he was employed on the Vanderbilt estate and could not leave.
biltmore-biltmore-1903-08-24.A3:
GOVERNOR AYCOCK'S CHOICE IS GORMAN
As Democratic Nominee He Thinks He Can Win.
TOBACCO TRUST MATTER
He Reports the Conduct of the Soldiers in Asheville as Being Excellent and Knows of No Threatened Clash of Races Trouble.
Trouble.
Governor Aycock was in his office yesterday, looking well after his trip to Asheville.

"Sorry to learn that you have been sick Governor," said the reporter, referring to the report of the Governor having had an attack of cholera morbus on the train coming from Asheville.

"It was only a slight attack," he replied. "Something I ate disagreed with me, and I am feeling all right today."

The conversation then turned to Presidential possibilities and in speaking of these Governor Aycock expressed his preference for Senator A. P. Gorman, of Maryland. He is strongly of the opinion that Mr. Gorman will be nominated by the Democratic party, and says that if this is done Mr. Gorman will be elected.

As to the opposing candidate of the Republicans he holds that the nomination of President Roosevelt would be the best thing for the Democrats. His view is that with Gorman as the Democratic nominee and Roosevelt as the Republican nominee the Democrats will win the victory.

Talking of his visit to Asheville Governor Aycock says that the behavior of the soldiers there, as he saw it, and heard of it, was excellent. With reference to the reported tossing of some negroes in blankets by the troops as they left he says that he heard nothing of it and if it was so that the matter was only that of a prank, with no harm intended and that there was nothing in it that had any tendency to a clash of the races.

Being asked concerning any proposed action on his part with regard to the resolution of the Farmers' Alliance concerning the controlling of the tobacco trust, and asking his co-operation with the Governors of South Carolina and Virginia in asking the President of the United States to inforce any laws in existence against such monopoly Governor Aycock said he was investigating the matter, and that he would as soon as possible take some steps in line with the request made of him.

Lynching Party on the Trail.

Harmony Grove, Ga., Nov. 24.—With a determination that bodes but a short life to the young men, if caught, posses of both blacks and whites are searching for three white men named Chandler, McGinnis and Fitzpatrick. The crime with which they are charged is torturing and criminally assaulting a negress from whose bosom they first tore her infant. It is an open statement that lynching will follow the capture of the men.
chandler-harmony-grove-1903-11-21.A2:
THREE WHITE MEN OUTRAGE WOMAN

A Horrible Crime is Committed in Madison County
THE EXCITEMENT IS INTENSE
Dragged Woman From Her Home and Kept Off Would-be Rescuers With Guns.—Great Excite- citement over the Affair.
Harmony Grove, Ga., Nov. 24.—One of the most horrible crimes ever committed in this section was perpetrated 3 miles below this place in Madison county last Saturday night about 9 o'clock.

Three young white men, Chandler, McGinnis and Fitzpatrick, went to the home of a negro in which there was two women and one man, broke the door down, threw the babe from the young mother's arms, dragged her out of the house and took her into the field about one hundred yards and mercilessly assaulted her.

They kept her there in awful agony for two hours. Neighbors heard her screams and went to the scene of the terrible crime, but the young men were armed and would not allow them to interfere. They were forced to remain at a distance and witness the assault and near the screams and prayers of the woman.

The young men finally left the woman in a hopeless condition and she had to be carrried home. It is said that they were under the influence of liquor.

Warrants have been issued and officers are seaching for the young men, and it is thought that they will be captured tonight.

There is considerable excitement in this section and the people are very much wrought up over the horrible crime.

HORRIBLE CRIME IS CHARGED.
Three White Men Outraged Negro Woman Near Harmony Grove.
Woman Near Harmony Grove.

Harmony Grove, Ga., November 23. (Special.)—One of the most horrible crimes ever committed in this section was perpetrated 3 miles below this place in Madison county last Saturday night about 9 o'clock.

Three young white men, Chandler, McGinnis and Fitchpatrick, went to the home of a negro in which there were two women and one man, broke the door down, threw the babe from the young mother's arms, dragged her out of the house and took her into the field about 100 yards from the house, and mercilessly assaulted her.

They kept her there in awful agony for two hours. Neighbors heard her screams and went to the scene of the terrible crime, but the young men were armed and would not allow them to interfere. They were forced to stand at a distance and witness the assault and hear the screams and prayers of the woman.

The young men finally left the woman in a helpless condition and she had to be carried back to her home. It is said that they were under the influence of liquor.
chandler-harmony-grove-1903-11-21.A7:
Ought to Be Hung.
At Harmony Grove, Ga., Chandler, McGennis and Fitchpatrick, all white men, went to the home of a negro woman after nightfall and at the point of drawn weapons forced her to go into a nearby field, where they criminally assaulted her. Neighbors of the woman heard her screams and rushed to the scene, but at the point of guns they were kept from interfering. She was finally left in a precarious condition and was soon picked up by friends and carried back to her house. Warrants have been sworn out for the young men, and every means possible will be taken to capture them. It is said that they were under the influence of whiskey. The town has been thrown into a pit of excitement over the affair.

The southern judiciary are doing something to redeem the reputation of their section. Judge Jones has a worthy fellow in Judge Speer, who at Savannah, Tuesday, passed sentence on two men who had pleaded guilty to 13 charges of an indictment for holding negroes in peonage. He imposed a fine of $2000 on each in two of the cases, and suspended sentence in the other 11, which hang over their heads as a warning. Judge Speer is quoted as commending the return of the indictments for indicating "an absence of race prejudice." This curiously sets forth what the practice down South is. A grand jury in the North would hardly be complimented by a judge for finding an indictment on the facts. But Judge Speer took occasion to disown the shotgun idea of Senator Tillman's speech in Savannah, a few evenings before. These paragraphs are worth quoting:—

Now, there is a peculiar obligation upon our southern white people to do all we can for the betterment of this race which is among us, which was formerly servile and yet which forms so important a part of our economy. Most of them are ignorant, many of them are degraded, but it is the Christian duty of every white man in the South to do all he can to give the negro a fair chance. I know the kindliness and the considerate temper of the southern people toward the negroes. They are the very best friends the negroes have. They give them an opportunity to live, an opportunity to work at any trade; they protect them, and the negro will feel safe in submitting any case to a jury composed of southern gentlemen, no matter how serious the charge. Some talk wildly and extravagantly about the shotgun policy, but they do not represent the gentlemen of the South.

The national civil-service reform league will hold their annual meeting at Baltimore, December 10-11. The sessions will be held at Lyric hall, excepting one on Thursday afternoon, the 10th, which will be at McCoy hall of Johns Hopkins university, and will be addressed by prominent persons, whose names will be published later. At the first public meeting, that morning, reports will be given, among them those of the special committees on the civil service in dependencies and on consular reform, and from the women's auxiliaries. The Maryland women immediately follow with a luncheon to "delegates and ladies accompanying them." In the evening the meeting will be addressed by Dr D. C. Gilman, president of the league, John R. Proctor, president of the United States civil-service commission, and William Dudley Foulke, while Charles J. Bonaparte will preside. The first session of Friday morning will be for election and business; next in the afternoon papers will be read on "The need of greater efforts and more effective methods in advocating the merit system," by Charles Richardson; "The merit principle in selection of the higher municipal officers," by Richard Henry Dana; "Fourth-class postmasters and rural free delivery," by Elliot H. Goodwin, secretary of the league; with discussion of each paper. Also a dinner given by the civil-service reform association of Maryland will be discussed in the evening, closing the annual meeting.

The appraisal of the estate of C. P. Huntington, just made public, makes it net $26,505,540 in personal property and $1,796,225 in realty located in New York state. Additional would be real estate in California and elsewhere of unknown amount. Most of the personal property is in stocks and bonds of railroads in the Southern Pacific system. His luxurious tastes appear to have run to pictures largely, for those in the Fifty-seventh-street mansion are valued at $464,825, those in the Westchester house at $27,310 and those in the San Francisco residence at $187,385; while only $12,000 is found in private railroad cars and only $3000 in a steam yacht. His estate was commonly supposed to be worth some $70,000,000, but proves, as is generally the case, to fall far short of the popular supposition. Still it has undergone a great shrinkage within a year, the large amount of stock of the Southern Pacific company having declined nearly one-half in market value from the highest of last year.

One of Speaker Cannon's special difficulties is in making up the House committee on labor. The labor unions have demanded direct representation upon it, and, in gratifying this desire, the speaker has aimed to make the committee represent non-union labor and farm labor as well, while at the same time insuring conservative action in whatever the committee may do. The oddity of the affair, as it finally turns out, is that the representative of labor unionism on the committee is to be W. R. Hearst, the millionaire newspaper publisher. Mr Hearst appears to be the choice, moreover, of the labor organizations, so far as their sentiment could be gathered.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 5.—Postmaster General Payne received information to-day that a posse of white citizens at Boeuf river, Louisiana, last night ordered Charles Jackson, a negro mail carrier, not to return with the mail on his route, and threatened him with death in case he did not heed their injunction. Senator McLaurin, of Mississippi, to-day conferred with Postmaster General Payne on the situation at Indianola, Miss., where the postoffice has been closed as a result of antagonism to the negro postmaster. Subsequently Senator McLaurin stated that he believed the office would be reopened this week. Mr. Payne said the office will be reopened if there is no intimidation of the postmaster.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., Jan. 5.—A special to the Courier-Journal from Indianola, Miss., says: "Mrs. Minnie Cox, the colored postmaster of this place, on account of whose resignation the government ordered the postoffice here closed, left Indianola tonight for Birmingham, Ala., accompanied by her mulatto assistant. It is now thought there is little danger of further trouble and, although the sentiment of the people is against the action of the government in closing the office on account of the consequent partial paralysis of business, no violence is anticipated. Before she left to-night Mrs. Cox made a statement in which she denied that she had been subjected to any indignities and stated that no violence had been threatened her. She said, however, that she would not again take the office of postmaster under any circumstances. Her husband, who is employed in the United States railway mail service, also made a statement in which he said that his wife had not been threatened, but that he understood the race problem in the South, and had advised her to give up the place. 'There is no doubt,' he continued, 'that there is a general sentiment here against a negro postmaster.'

New York Evening Post: Obviously the infirmities of human nature lies at the root of the labor problem, and since you cannot expel nature with a fork you cannot settle the problem by any formula what. ever. We cannot go back far enough in the history of free people to find time or place where the labor problem was not rife and vexing. Only in slaveholding times and countries has the problem been wanting, but there its place has been filled by injustice and cruelty at which civilization shudders. Shall we never have the labor problem settled, then? No; we shall never see a time when men will not have disputes with each other about the division of the point product of labor and capital. Not even socialism, if it were practicable, would bring that to pass, because socialism would not eliminate selfishness from the human breast. And who can say that it would be desirable to eliminate selfishness from human motives? Although its grosser forms are shocking and repulsive it remains true so that the desire to better one's own conditions the motive which keeps the world going. It lies at the bottom of material progress everywhere and is consistent with the highest type of altruism and generosity. We cannot conceive of a world void of that motive. But although the labor problem may never be settled the bad feature of it may be mitigated. Its evil consequences may be reduced to a minimum by frank and good tempered conferences, helping either side to look at the subject from the other's point of view and loading to conciliations and aribration rather than force as the umpire between them.

The situation of Indianola, Miss., growing out of opposition to Mrs. Minnie Cox continuing as postmistress, because of her color, is somewhat modified by her statement that in no circumstances will she accept the postoffice again.

According to the decision of the Cabinet. the officers at Indianola decided to leave Mrs. Cox in undisturbed possession, and this decision followed the sending of her resignation. Now, however, that Mrs. Cox absolutely and finallywithdraws the President may appoint- a new post master and reopen the office.

But this will no settle the trouble that has grown out of the case in other parts of the South. A wave of

sentiment against negro officeholders appears to have been set in motion, and it would be difficult to say where it will reach its height.

The "simple request"—which was, in fact, a threat—that Mrs. Cox resign was signed by more than fifty business and professional men of Indianola. Mrs. Cox and her husband understood the meaning between the lines; they knew there was "a general sentiment against the reign of a negro postmaster;" they "understood" the race problem and they agreed that the safest thing for Mrs. Cox to do, was to quit.

And now the people of Indianola have opened an independent post office supported by private contributions. This is contrary to federal law, though not at variance with common sense. A posse of whites in Louisina has given a negro mail carrier warning that if he does not quit the service he will be killed. The State Democratic organ of New Orleans, has called the President a "czar" and added this plain threat: "His negro appointees will be killed just as the negro appointees of other Republican Presidents have been put out of the way."

Is not this a deplorable state of affairs? Because the President allows a negro woman to retain an office which she has held without open opposition for six years, or appoints negro citizens to place under the government, as is his and their right "leading business men" make requests(?) that they quit, and a leading newspaper openly threatens murder and brazenly admits that murder has already been done. And all because of difference in color!

Where will all this end? Who will eventually yield, the nation government or the lawless mob element of the South? Does the South hope to settle the nergo problem by intimidating violence and murder?—Chicago Evening Post.

As the whites hold all the state and local offices in the South they ought not to object to the occasional appointment of a colored person to a federal office for which he is qualified. In many localities and in some Southern States the negroes outnumber the whites, and as some of them are qualified to hold office it would be gross injustice to exclude them from doing so solely on the ground of color. The present protest is the more surprising because for many years past colored men have been holding federal offices in the South without exciting much opposition. The case of the Indianola (Miss.) postoffice has given that obscure town more notoriety than it ever could have obtained by decent or lawful means. Mrs. Cox, the colored woman who was forced to resign the office, was not an original appointee of President Roosevelt's. She had filled the office eight years to the entire satisfaction of the department and had shown herself capable and trustworthy. Nothing was alleged against her by the Indianola people but her color. When she was forced to resign and was virtually driven out of the town the postmaster general ordered the office closed, and now the people are furious because they have to send to Greenville, twenty-five miles distant, for their mail. The order is denounced by the white citizens of Indianola as a piece of "peanut" politics, and they say they will allow the postoffice to remain closed for all time before they will permit the administration at Washington to force a black postmaster upon them. If the rowdy element of Indianola only knew it, the closing of the postoffice is a mild punishment for their conduct. Section 5518 of the Revised Statutes of the United States reads as follows:

If two or more persons in any State or Territory conspire to prevent by force, intimidation or threat any person from accepting or holding any office, trust or place of confidence under the United States or from discharging any duties thereof, or to induce by like means any officer of the United States to leave a State, district or place where his duties as an officer are required to be performed, or to injure him in his person or property on account of his lawful discharge of the duties of his office, or while engaged in the lawful discharge thereof, or to injure his property so as to molest, interrupt, hinder or impede him in the discharge of his official duties, each of such persons shall be punished by a fine of not less than $500 or more than $5,000, or by imprisonment, with or without hard labor, not less than six months nor more than six years, or by both such fine and imprisonment.

Prosecution in the United States Court under this section might cause the conspirators much more inconvenience than the closing of the postoffice. It is, of course, unfortunate that the closing of the office punishes the innocent citizens of Indianola as well as the guilty, but as the whole community seems to be standing together it will not hurt them to realize that the government is master of the situation. The incident has caused a good deal of comment, by far the most violent being from the New Orleans States, a Democratic organ. That paper says:

In discussing the Indianola postoffice incident we do not believe it to be wise for either the people of the South or their newspapers to mince words. President Roosevelt in closing the postoffice at Indianola has suspended the law for the deliberate purpose of offending and insulting the white people of the South, and incidentally to pander to the negro vote of the Northern pivotal States. He has assumed the role of a czar for the sole purpose of cinching the presidential nomination in 1904, and it is well that the South should proclaim its knowledge of his motives and also to impress upon the mind of the country the fact that if President Roosevelt has made up his mind to outrage and insult people of the South by appointing and keeping in office obnoxious negroes his negro appointees will be killed just as the negro appointees of other Republican Presidents have been put out of the way. Some persons will say, no doubt, that these are intemperate and violent views, but we are confident that they will be indorsed by the majority of the people in the Southern States. It may be said also that if Mr. Roosevelt's negro appointees are killed or run out of the country he will dragoon the South with federal troops. In such an event we are confident that the fact will be quickly established that our people are fully as strenuous as their Knickerbocker President. The people of the South were dragooned during the "dark days of reconstruction," and the history of that period shows that they did some dragooning on their own account. It was effective then, and it is well for the President to know that it will be still more effective now. If he desires, in order to serve his own political ends, to raise "a rough house" in the South he can rest assured that the game will be made entirely interesting for him.

From this one might suppose that President Roosevelt had inaugurated a new policy, but he has done nothing of the kind. Every Republican President for thirty years past has appointed some colored persons to office in the South as well as in the North, and in proportion to the colored population more in the North than in the South. Such talk as that above quoted will not be likely to deter the President from doing what he thinks is just and right. Since the Indianola office was closed the postmaster general has received information that a mob of white men at Beef River, La., ordered a negro mail carrier not to return with the mail on his route or they would kill him. There are hundreds of colored letter carriers and railway mail clerks in the North, and people never think of questioning their right to hold office. In Charleston, S. The President told them that if they could bring anything affecting his character or fitness he would hear them. They brought charges, but failed to establish them, so the President appointed him. FIENDISH Was the Murder of Mrs. Alice Matthews. HACKED TO PIECES WITH AX AFTER SHE HAD BEEN CRIMINALLY ASSAULTED. LITTLE DAUGHTER MANGLED. Negro Against Whom Evidence Was Strong Shot To Death While Running Away. ONCE LIVED IN LOUISVILLE. Shreveport, La., April 11.—[Special.] —Mrs. Alice Matthews, aged forty-five years, wife of Frank Matthews, a well-known engineer, was brutally murdered in her bed early this morning by a negro who, it is believed, outraged his victim before slaying her. The woman's little daughter Aline, aged ten, was probably fatally wounded. An ax was the instrument employed in both cases. Ed Porter, a negro strongly suspected of the crime, was shot to death by two police sergeants while attempting to escape. He had been run down at a point about five miles from Shreveport. Discovery of the Crime.
The discovery of the crime was made at 5:30 o'clock this morning by a servant who entered the bedroom of Mrs. Matthews. The unfortunate woman, who was almost hacked to pieces, had been dead for some time. Her daughter was still alive when the servant entered. Entrance was effected through a side window, and although there were fifteen persons in the house, which is situated in the very heart of the residence district of Shreveport, no one heard a single suspicious sound during the night.

Had Been Assaulted.

The skull of Mrs. Matthews was crushed and she bore evidence of having been criminally assaulted. The child's skull was fractured, her chest crushed and shoulder lacerated. Mrs. Matthews wore a diamond ring and diamond earrings, which were not touched by the murderer, and three pocketbooks containing money were in the room, showing that criminal assault furnished the motive for the crime. An ax covered with blood and hair was found in the kitchen.

Negro Shot To Death.

Bloodhounds took up the trail of the murderer, but lost it after going a short distance. A Kansas City Southern engineer notified the police of the appearance of a negro covered with blood on the tracks of the railroad and a posse was organized to hunt him down. The posse separated and Sergeants Gerald and Roquemore soon came upon the negro. He made a desperate dash for a ravine and the officers fired four shots at him, two of which took effect in his back, killing him instantly. The negro's clothing was covered with blood and his shoes fitted the bloody footprints in the kitchen of the Matthews home. His name was Ed Porter, and he was a well-known Shreveport negro.

Came From Louisville.

Mrs. Alice Matthews, the victim of the murder and outrage, resided upwards of five years in Shreveport, coming here from Louisville. She was a Miss Hicks, of Somerset, Ky. A brother, Robert Hicks, resides at Birmingham, Ala., and a telegram was sent to him, telling of his sister's murder, with the request that he break the news to the woman's husband, who has a run as engineer out of Anniston, Ala., over the Seaboard Airline. Mrs. Matthews was held in the highest esteem here and her tragic death was a terrible shock to friends and acquaintances. The little girl is still alive, with a remote chance of recovery. Later to-day the child was operated on and a piece of the skull removed.

REPUBLICAN BOLT IN OMAHA CONVENTION.

Seventy-One Delegates Will Not Stand For Mayor Moores' Third Term Nomination.

Omaha, Neb., April 11—The Republicans to-day nominated Mayor Moores for re-election, and thereby precipitated a bolt of seventy-one delegates, who say that they will nominate a ticket of their own on Monday. The convention was so uproarious that the police were called in twice to quell the obstreperous delegates.

Mayor Moores was nominated for a third term on the first ballot by one vote. After eight wards had been called and voted, Chairman Goss, of the Ninth ward, demanded a poll of the Second ward. The chairman ignored him and ordered the secretary to proceed with the roll call. The convention was soon in an uproar, the police flocked on to the floor to preserve order, and forcibly pushed a number of the delegates into their seats. Those opposed to Moores' men said the chairman was arbitrary in his ruling, and when the chairman declared Moores nominated seventy-one delegates bolted. After the withdrawal of these delegates the remainder of the ticket was nominated by the regular convention.

Labor Troubles Over.

Labor Troubles Over. Cannelton, Ind., April 11.—[Special.]— The labor troubles which have existed during the past two years at the mines of the American Cannel Coal Company here have been amicably settled, and

the old men who were formerly employed are expected to return to their places in the mines next Tuesday. This will add to coal shipments on the Ohio.

JOHN H. PUNCH DIES
AT MT. STERLING.

Had Served For Several Years As Deputy Warden of the Frankfort Penitentiary.

Mt. Sterling, Ky., April 11.—[Special.]
—John Henry Punch, De puty Warden of the penitentiary at Frankfort, died at his home in this city to-day at 5 o'clock p. m. The funeral services will be held at St. Patrick's church, this city, Tuesday morning at 10 o'clock and the interment will be at Mt. Sterling.

Mr. Punch was thirty-one years old and left a wife and one child, a son four and one-half years old. He was a son of the late Capt. Patrick Punch, who had held various places of public trust and was United States Deputy Marshal under Capt. James Blackburn, John Henry Punch was a merchant here until he accepted the position of Deputy Warden under Col. Eph Lillard, succeeding the late Edward McGrath.

OFFICERS OF GEORGIA
BANK INDICTED.

President and Vice President of Warrenton Bank Charged With Wrecking the Concern.

Washington, Ga., April 11.—The grand jury of Warren county to-day returned indictments against W. S. Witham, of Atlanta, former president and financial agent, and E. B. Farmer, vice president of the bank at Warrenton, which institution closed its doors in February, 1902, owing to depositors some $16,000. The indictments charged felony in rendering the bank insolvent and loaning more than 10 per cent. of the capital stock to one officer of the bank.

MOB AFTER NEGRO

WHO STRUCK WHITE MAN AT INDIANAPOLIS.

Race War Would Have Followed,
But For Interference of Police
With Revolvers.

Indianapolis, April 11.—A fight between two white men and a negro at 5:30 o'clock this evening precipitated a race riot and the negro, Clifford Ball, a lad about twenty years old, narrowly escaped violence at the hands of a mob of a hundred men.

After striking one of the men, John Bush, on the head with a brick, knocking him senseless to the sidewalk, Ball ran south, pursued by half a dozen men. The crowd increased to a hundred, and cries of "lynch him" were heard as the mob pursued the flying negro through the streets. Policemen with drawn revolvers saved him.

EARTHQUAKE SHOCK
IN CITY OF MEXICO.

People Rushed Into the Streets In
Fright, But No Serious Damage
Is Reported.

Mexico City, April 11.—At 9:15 p. m. a sharp earthquake shock was felt in this city. Some excitement prevailed for a time, many people rushing into the street, fearing that the earthquake might prove serious. No damage resulted, however. It is not known whether the shock was felt in other portions of the republic.

Mazatlan, Mex., April 11.—There are now but two patients at the lazaretto, both of whom are rapidly improving. One man has died of the plague at the lazaretto at Siquieros. All other patients at that place are making quick recoveries.

BAD NEGROES COMING NORTH.
Southern Cities Driving Out the Loafers and Criminals.
NEW ORLEANS, June 26.—The movement started in several parts of the South to get rid of the disorderly negro element responsible for most of the recent crimes in this section is gaining strength, and it is likely to become general instead of spasmodic, as formerly, and unload a large number of negro gamblers, confidence men and other criminals on the North.

The towns in southern Mississippi are following the example of Ellisville and Laurel in this matter, and ordering out all negro criminals, tramps and dangerous characters. Cooper, in Delta county, has started the movement in Texas. The negro loafers, negro sneak thieves and petty criminals of that town have been taken out by the Regulars, whipped and ordered to leave town.

Taking advantage of the excitement caused by the whipping, the houses of some of the better class negroes were placarded with notices to leave. They complained to the authorities, and at a joint meeting held at the court house the whites pledged their support to all orderly negroes, the negroes on their part promising to do all in their power to keep down the lawless element and to report all violators of law among the negroes to the authorities.

An investigation disclosed the fact that the warnings on the houses of the negroes were placed there by mischievous boys.
cooper-cooper-1903-06.A2: Some of the southern cities and villages are undertaking to drive all the disorderly negroes out of that part of the country and unload them on the north. This is right in line with the police policy the country over of turning criminals loose on condition that they get out of town. These negro criminals will not be in the north long before they will be rounded up, and where the negro population is sparse they will not have such a field for their evil work as in the south. It is reassuring to notice, however, that the enforced exodus does not apply to the orderly negro population. At Cooper, Delta county, Texas, the whites have pledged protection to all orderly negroes, and the latter have agreed to do all in their power to repress the disorderly element and to report to the authorities all violators of law among them. If this agreement is lived up to on both sides there will be much more mutual respect in Delta and a much better condition of race relations.

— The Brown cotton concern is bringing a great deal of queer cotton to New Orleans, says a dispatch of June 27, from that city. Cotton has become so valuable that the owners of gins are scraping the floors and have made up several bales of waste cotton. Perhaps the most extraordinary bale, however, is one that arrived here today from Georgia. It is of the crop of 1872, and is consequently 31 years old. Its owner held out for 16 cents that year, but when the market broke and cotton went down, he swore he would never sell it for less than 16 cents. When cotton went up to 14 cents in New Orleans he shipped it here, to be ready for the 16 cents he pledged himself to, with orders to his agent to sell whenever that figure was reached. The cotton has been stored in a room for thirty-one years and is thoroughly dried out, having lost fifty pounds in the process of drying. Experts declare the staple to be as good as ever.

— Knoxville, Tenn., dispatch of June 27: Harvey Logan, the alleged Montana train robber, under sentence of twenty years, escaped from the Knox county jail this afternoon at 5 o'clock. While his guard's back was turned, Logan threw a wire over his head and lassoed him, tieing him tight to the bars of his cage. Having one entire floor of the jail to himself, Logan next secured two pistols placed in the corridor of the jail for use by officers if needed. When Jailor Bell appeared in answer to a call from Logan the prisoner passed out a bottle, saying he wanted some medicine. As the jailer put out his hand Logan covered him with a pistol, forced him to unlock the door and take him to the basement of the jail. He then forced Bell to take him to the sheriff's stable and saddle the sheriff's horse. This done, Logan mounted and rode away in the direction of the mountains. A posse started in pursuit of the desperado within one hour. Sheriff J. W. Fox tonight offered a reward of $500 for the capture of Logan, dead or alive.

— New Orleans dispatch of June 26: The movement started in several parts of the south to get rid of the disorderly Negro element responsible for most of the recent crimes in this section is gaining strength, and it is likely to become general instead of spasmodic, as formerly, and unload a large number of Negro gamblers, confidence men and other criminals on the north. The towns in southern Mississippi are following the example of Ellisville and Laurel in this matter, and ordering out all Negro criminals, tramps and dangerous characters. Cooper, in Delta county, has started the movement in Texas. The Negro loafers, Negro sneak thieves and petty criminals of that town have been taken out by the regulars, whipped and ordered to leave town. Taking advantage of the excitement caused by the whipping, the houses of some of the better class Negroes were placarded with notices to leave. They complained to the authorities, and at a joint meeting held at the court house the whites pledged their support to all orderly Negroes, the Negroes on their part promising to do all in their power to keep down the lawless element and to report all violators of law among the Negroes to the authorities. An investigation disclosed the fact that the warnings on the houses of the Negroes were placed there by mischievous boys.

cooper-cooper-1903-06.A5:
Insolent Negroes Given a Flogging
Citizens Warn Worthless Blacks to Leave Cooper, Texas
Dallas, Tex.: Reports from Cooper, in Delta County, state that much excitement and anxiety exist there because of a race conflict, which may grow to serious proportions.

For a week notices have been posted in conspicuous places warning negroes to leave Cooper or take the consequences. Last Wednesday night three negro leaders were taken from their homes and severely flogged. Three others had been whipped a week previously. The flogged negroes were compelled to leave the county. They are charged with having made insolent criticism of the trial and life sentence given a negro named Walker two weeks ago for attempting to assault a white woman.

A meeting of leading white and black citizens was held at Cooper Thursday night. The white men assured the negroes that the well-behaved could remain and be protected, but that the worthless, insolent and dangerous negroes would have to go. Officers are searching for the men who did the flogging.

Durante la útima semana se han colocado carteles en los sitios públicos mas concurridos disponiendo que los negros del condado salgan inmediatamente o que de lo contrario se atengan à las consecuencias de su temeridad. eldorado-eldorado-1903-02.A1:
NEGROES ARE DRIVEN OUT OF PENNSYLVANIA TOWN
Washington, February 26.—(Special.)—Southern senators are greatly interested in a report from Indiana, Penn., detailing how the whole negro population of the town had been driven out because of a crime of one negro. In speaking of the incident today Senator Tillman said: "This event only goes to illustrate what I said in my speech that the northern white man has no no more love for the negro than the southern white man has. "I think the incursion of negroes to the north is teaching a very practical lesson to the northern white man. The northern white man does not want the
eldorado-eldorado-1903-02.A2:
negro. I lectured in the middle west some time ago, and I can point out at least eight towns in the state of Indiana, for instance, where they won't allow a negro to land. When a black immigrant comes along they say to him, 'You are all right and you are just as good as we are, but move along we don't want you.'

"The people of Eldorado, Ill., recently chased every negro out of the town. The northern white man knows the negro as well as we do, but won't acknowledge it.

"President McKinley changed his race policy before he died. He acknowledged that the only hope for the negro was in industrial development.
eldorado-eldorado-1903-02.A3:
HEADACHES Cured While You Wait, By CAPUDINE NO EFFECT ON THE HEART. Sold at all Drug Stores.
Want No Negroes North.
Washington, February 27.—Senator Tillman to-day emphasized his magnificent speech of Tuesday on the race question by making a few pertinent observations on the action of citizens of Indiana, Pa., in driving negroes from the town. He was shown a copy of press reports of the Pennsylvania "outrage" upon the negro, and he said:

"It has become to be recognized that the negroes who are entering the North are carrying with them a better knowledge of the race and that the Northern people will rule them out altogether. You can see that demonstrated right here in the District of Columbia. We have disfranchised the negro because we do not want his rule and domination, but the Federal authorities wink at it.

"I repeat that the white man of the North does not care any more for the black man than the white man of the South does. McKinley was forced to change his views before he died. He was fooled at first on the question.

"He said finally that the negro must rely on industrial development for his future.

"I know of at least eight towns in Indiana where the people will not allow a negro immigrant to step off a train. They do not want the black man, and when he comes along they tell him to move on."
