fletcher-hollis-smyrna-1903-08-03.A1:
HUNTED BY THREE POSSES
Delaware Town Infuriated by Negro Desperado.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

Smyrna, Del., Aug. 3.—This State is on the eve of another lynching. Three hundred men armed with shotguns and revolvers, in three posses, are pursuing Fletcher Hollis, twenty-three years old, a desperate negro of this place, who to-night shot and fatally wounded Constable James D. Wright, at Clayton, one mile from here, while resisting arrest. Clayton was so excited over the shooting that the negro managed to get away, after holding several pursuers at bay with his pistol. As the negro is well known his capture either to-night or tomorrow is confidently looked for.

The posses, which are led by Benjamin Turner, Chief of Police; Policeman Joseph Cummins and Constable Charles H. Jones, all of Smyrna, and W. D. Venn and William King, of Clayton, are guarding every avenue of escape for a radius of a half dozen miles and they will spend the night on guard. If they catch the negro it is conceded that he will be shot.

Constable Jones, of Smyrna, and Constable Wright, of Clayton, were co-operating in an effort to arrest Hollis on the double charge of shooting at a man in Dover last Saturday night and of creating a disturbance at the Friendship (colored) camp meeting, four miles from here, last evening. Unfortunately, neither constable was armed. When they saw the negro in front of the Hotel Stockle, in Clayton, this evening, Wright approached and said to the negro:

"I want you!"

"No, you don't want me," was the reply.

"Oh, yes, I do, and I will take you," Wright said.

At this juncture the negro drew a revolver and aimed it at Wright's head, shouting: "You won't take me!"

Wright, who, up to this time, had not been assisted by Constable Jones, because of the latter's failure to have a pistol, seized the negro and wheeled him around. Wright hoped by doing this he would have the revolver pointed away from him. Before he could accomplish this, however, Hollis pulled the trigger, and the bullet entered his victim's abdomen. Wright, who is fifty years old, walked to the hotel steps, where he collapsed and was carried inside and physicians summoned.

Constable Jones secured a revolver from a bystander and started after the fleeing negro. As soon as he fired Hollis ran toward Smyrna, pointing his weapon over his shoulder and warning his pursuers to keep back. He soon entered a cornfield and started across country. Word was sent by telephone in all directions to catch the slayer, and the organization of the posses followed.

Hollis went in the direction of Smyrna River, which runs into Delaware Bay near Woodland Beach, and the posses followed him closely. At 9 o'clock to-night it was believed that he was surrounded in a cornfield near the head of the river, but if such was the case the negro eluded his pursuers. He owns a small boat, which is moored in the neighborhood.

It was reported late to-night that he had succeeded in reaching the boat and was rowing for the bay. The river is very circuitous, and members of the posses are on the banks watching with guns. They all know the negro, and they declare that if they see him they will shoot to kill without asking questions.

It is possible that the desperado, who is familiar with the country, is hiding in the swamp, in which case he will probably not be seen until daylight.

It was reported here shortly before midnight that Hollis was in the negro quarter of the town, and that two of his friends had a team ready to take him away, but an armed crowd failed to verify the rumor.

Hollis is a desperate character of Smyrna and has given the authorities much trouble.

Constable Wright is a Democratic leader of Kent County, and was recently re-elected to his office by the Kent County levy court, which is Republican. He will be taken to the Delaware Hospital in Wilmington early to-morrow morning. The people are enraged because the tragedy of to-night occurred on the same spot where three years ago Herbert Haynes, night watchman, of Clayton, was killed by a negro tramp, who was never captured.
fletcher-hollis-smyrna-1903-08-03.A4:
WRIGHT MAY RECOVER.
Two Posses Are Searching for Man Who Shot Him.
Who Shot Him.

WILMINGTON, Del., August 4. It was stated at the Delaware Hospital today that Constable James D. Wright of Clayton, Del., who was last night shot and seriously wounded by Fletcher Hollis, a negro desperado whom he was about to arrest at Clayton, would probably recover.

The news from Clayton is to the effect that the search for Hollis is still being vigorously continued and that it is probable that he will be shot to death if he is apprehended. State Detective Francis is on the scene, and if the negro is caught will endeavor to place him in custody and bring him to this city for safekeeping.

The searching parties, however, say they do not propose to allow this to be done. There are two of them, each numbering about one hundred men, and they are patrolling the banks of the Smyrna river from Clayton to Bombay Hook in search of Hollis, who is supposed to be hiding in the marshes.
fletcher-hollis-smyrna-1903-08-03.A13:
CONSTABLE WRIGHT SHOT WHILE ARRESTING HOLLIS
NEGRO WHIPPED OUT A REVOLVER AND FIRED BULLET INTO WRIGHTS STOMACH.
He Then Made His Escape and Is Still at Large. Great Indignation in Clayton and Smyrna and a Posse Formed to Capture Him.

While attempting to arrest Fletcher Hollis, a young negro, Monday evening, Constable James D. Wright, of Clayton, was shot in the abdomen, and it is believed almost fatally wounded. Hollis then made his escape. The shooting occurred near the Delaware railroad station at Clayton about 6.30 o'clock in the evening. Constable Wright and Constable Jones, of Smyrna, had been looking for Hollis and Monday they received word that he was in Clayton. The officers went to the railroad station where he was supposed to be and after a short search found him in company with some colored people. Hollis was arrested on a charge of shooting at Dover and another charge of breaking the peace at Mt. Friendship camp-meeting, near Clayton, on Sunday evening.

Constable Wright approached the group and telling Hollis he was wanted laid his hand on his shoulder. At this instant Hollis whipped out a revolver and fired at Constable Wright. The bullet took effect in the abdomen, and the official fell to the ground with a moan. Several persons witnessed the scene but the shooting was so sudden it took them unawares.

Hollis Lost No Time in Making Escape.

Hollis, on firing the shot, made a dash for liberty and soon outdistanced the crowd of pursuers, led by Constable Jones. In the meantime a number of persons had gone to the assistance of the wounded constable and carried him to the Stoeckle Hotel, near to the place of the shooting, and a physician summoned. It was soon seen that his injuries were very serious, and Drs. Harmonson and Grier were called in attendance. At first the physicians had but little hope for the recovery of the injured man, but later in the evening they gave out a statement in which they said that his condition was more hopeful.

Great indignation in Clayton and Smyrna.

The news of the shooting spread rapidly and Clayton and Smyrna was soon agog with excitement. Constable Jones and a searching party scoured the section round about for a trace of the fugitive, a posse of over a hundred men was made up at Smyrna, and the creek from a point near Clayton as far down as Smyrna Landing was thoroughly searched. Hollis was known to have a boat and some thought he might have rowed down the creek and escaped. Others felt he was near. In the meantime his colored friends drove around in a team and it is supposed gave him every assistance. The officers are firmly of the belief that they disguised Hollis in woman's clothes and drove him off up the State road. This story is borne out from the statement that a carriage stopped in front of the old Stockly barrack near the Bombay Hook railroad, a low whistle was given, and a figure in woman's apparel jumped boldly out from behind the building, got in the carriage and was driven off in the direction of Middletown. The bosse, however, continued their search until about midnight, but without result. Indignation was at a high pitch and had he been captured he would have been severely dealt with, if not trung up to the nearest tree. Yesterday Detectives Francis and Rutledge, of Wilmington, came down to work up the case. They visited Clayton and Smyrna, obtained all the information they could about Hollis, but at this writing they have no clue to his whereabouts. A description of the fugitive has been telegraphed to offices all over the State and Governor Hunn has strengthened the situation by offering $100 reward.

fletcher-hollis-smyrna-1903-08-03.A14:
Tendency of Negroes to Shoot Gives Rise to Determination to Make Example of Hollis
Smyrna Colored People So Alarmed That They Will Not Venture Out Unless Compelled
Smyrna, Aug. 5.—Spurred on by the added incentive of $100 reward offered last night by Governor Hunn, the two armed posses that Monday night started after Fletcher Hollis, the negro who shot Constable James D. Wright, are still keenly on the hunt.

The search has been made with such thoroughness in the negro quarter today that Hollis' neighbors locked their doors early tonight and not a colored resident has been seen on the street, unless driven out by necessity. This alarm is due to the discovery that Hollis' escape was due largely to aid given him by some of his own race, and that he was harbored for a time by them.

One of the posses was within a few yards of the hunted man, but he dodged and got away. This was while he was hiding in the rear of James Viney's house on East street.

Asked China Potts For Aid.

Yesterday Hollis visited China Potts, a mail carrier, and begged him to lend a horse, that he might go to Middletown. Potts did not know then of the crime and simply drove the negro away, the man starting in the direction of Wilmington.

Despite the fact that he has relatives in Chester, Pa., and would perhaps make for that place, where he would be practically safe, it is believed that he is in the Duck Creek settlement, a village about a mile from here, and very likely still disguised as a woman, it being claimed that he has been seen in woman's garb.

State Detectives Francis and Ratledge are here, presumably directing the search, but it is known that they came by direction of Governor Hunn, who insists that there be no lynching this time and that the officers be held responsible for Hollis' safety if he is captured by either posse.

The anger of Wright's friends cooled a little yesterday when it was reported that the officer might recover, but the tendency of the negroes to shoot at the slightest provocation has also given rise to a determination that Hollis shall be made an example of even at the risk of a sacrifice of life on the part of the avengers.

Wright Very Popular.

Constable Wright is probably one of the best-known peace officers in the county. A well-educated man and alert politician, he was a candidate for clerk of the peace of this county on the Democratic ticket during the last campaign. Because of his experience and knowledge of his district, the Republican Levy Court recently selected him, though a Democrat, for constable at Clayton, undoubtedly the most important post for a peace officer
fletcher-hollis-smyrna-1903-08-03.A15:
ARMED POSSE CONTINUES HUNT FOR DESPERADO
(Continued From First Page).
in the State, because of the location there of the Delaware railroad offices.

A large number of the negroes throughout this country are armed continually, and think nothing of firing their revolvers in the air. This state of affairs goes on in the face of repeated warnings from the courts. Chief Justice Lore has lost no opportunity to warn the negroes against the deadly weapon evil, but it continues without abatement.

Other Officers on the Trail.

Dover, Aug. 5.—Sheriff Melvin went to Milford with a view of heading off Hollis if he might be fleeing southward, and officers through the lower part of the county were also notified.

Deputy Constable Williams started from Dover yesterday with a trusty negro, one well acquainted with all the Kent county Afro-Americans and their places of abode. Williams arrested one negro as a suspicious character and found a weapon upon him that had been recently used. It is not likely, however, that the man whom he captured is Wright's assailant, as he was seen here about that time.

His Brothers Against Him.

Chester, Pa., Aug. 5.—Fletcher Hollis has three brothers in this city. They are William, David and Elwood, and all are employed at the Keystone Plaster Works, where they have a good reputation for sobriety and industry. All live in the western end of the city and when seen last night talked freely of the shooting. William was the chief spokesman and he said:

"Fletcher is our brother, and just how he came to get in this muss we don't know except what we saw in the papers. He never lived in Chester, and it has been a month since he was here. He was not in Chester last night to our knowledge. If he came here he did not come around to see us and we don't want to get into trouble with the police on his account. We don't uphold him in the shooting. Fletch is quick with the gun and we hope that if the men who are after him catch up with him that he don't have his weapon for he is a sure shot and it don't take him long to pull the trigger. There will be a bad fight if he is taken with his gun on him. What we care for most is our old father and mother."
Even if Hollis should come to Chester the police of this city would have no means of identifying him. No official notice of the crime has been received and no description of the man has been sent to the department. Chief Leary was prompt to act upon the meagre information he has received, but without result. It was said that Fletcher keeps company with a Chester girl, but William Hollis said last night that if that is true he has not heard of it. Constable Wright passed an easy night in Delaware Hospital and it is expected he will recover. All indications point to his getting well.
fletcher-hollis-smyrna-1903-08-03.A19: Events are verging on that point where the South will be constrained to rise up and deprecate lynchings. Because of the cause and the apparently futile effect we have always deplored it, but the fever seems to be spreading and if it continues at the rapid pace now set the time will soon come when the unfortunate African will have to seek other quarters or be stricken in his tracks. The North is now up in arms against the negro. Within a few weeks more lynchings have occurred north of the Mason and Dixon line than have occurred within the same period in the South because of the nameless crime. Strange to say, in Delaware, Indiana and Illinois mobs have sought or captured negroes, with lynching as a sequel when captured, not only for assault but for injury done white men or officials. This week three hundred armed men are scouring Delaware swamps for a negro who wounded a constable, and the lariat hangs conspicuously at the saddle pomel, while at the same time two negroes are being hunted in North Carolina for the most heinous offense on record. The worst feature of it all is that in some northern parts every man of black skin is being persecuted because of the sin of some worthless dastard of his race. So much is this so that whole colonies are fleeing for their lives and coming South. Oh, if only Harriet Beecher Stowe could rise up and see what her land is doing for her pets! She would swear by all the gods that roost on high Olympus that Uncle Tom and Topsy had both "growed" out of imagination. The only salvation for the peaceful and worthy negro that we can see is for him to suppress these outlaws of his race. The negro is with us, and in his proper sphere is acceptable and indispensable.

HOLLIS SEEN AT READING TERMINAL PHILADELPHIA
IDENTIFIED BY THE ARMSTRONGS FORMERLY OF SMYRNA, BUT NOT ARRESTED.
Local Officers Still on the Hunt and Saturday Night Several Properties Were Raid ed Without Gaining Additional Clues.
Fletcher Hollis, the negro desperado who brutally shot Constable James D. Wright of Clayton is still at large despite the efforts of the detectives and police officers to capture him. Saturday evening Detectives Francis and Rutledge came to Smyrna and in company with several men Clayton and Smyrna made a raid on the houses occupied by Moses Raisin, George Robinson and Steve Denby at "Irishtown" where it was thought Hollis might be concealed. They made their entrance about two o'clock Sunday morning and had not only the necessary warrants but were thoroughly armed to meet every emergency. Their search was fruitless and they left without obtaining any additional information. They also made a complete search of the Stockly barrack near the Bombay Hook Railroad but no trace of Hollis could be found. The detectives left on the 3.06 a. m. train for Wilmington. There have been many rumors as to Hollis' whereabouts, so many that it is absolutely confusing. One of the most plausible stories yet related was that Hollis was in this vicinity Saturday morning and taking a boat rowed out the Smyrna creek. Thomas Rench who had employed Hollis on frequent occasions declares that he saw Hollis going out the creek about 8 o'clock Saturday morning while he was crabbing. There has been a strong impression that Hollis has been around here all the time, but he cleverly evades the officers, and the $100 reward has not resulted so far in his capture.

Hollis Identified in Philadelphia Yesterday.

It has also been positively stated that Hollis visited East street after the shooting affair and concealed himself underneath an outbuilding in Jim Viney's yard and that he (Hollis) sent word to John Wick one of the leaders of the posse he was close enough at one time to shoot him down. Hollis is also said to have visited China Potts later and tried to hire a team which was refused. Yesterday the report came from Philadelphia that Hollis was seen at the Reading Terminal by Mr. J. C. Armstrong formerly of Smyrna, and later was seen by Mrs. Armstrong and a Mrs. Newman, both of whom knew him well. They notified a policeman that Hollis was desired for attempted murder, but the officer ignored them and made no attempt to arrest Hollis. Detectives Francis and Ratledge spent several hours running down clues, and they will start out again to-day, having gotten some additional tips last night that may prove valuable in landing Hollis.

Officers Throughout State Keeping Watch.

There was some excitement caused in Wilmington last Friday over a strange negro who made his appearance at Shellpot Park and from the description, the conductor and motorman of a trolley car were led to believe that it was Hollis. All over the state the officers are keeping a vigilant watch and the law abiding citizens are hoping that his capture will soon be effected. It is dangerous for a negro like Hollis to run at large

fletcher-hollis-smyrna-1903-08-03.A28:
FLETCHER HOLLIS FINALLY
JAILED AFTER LONG CHASE
SMYRNA NEGRO MUST PAY THE PENALTY FOR SHOOTING CONSTABLE WRIGHT.
Was Captured at Centreville, Md., by Robert Coursey and Taken to Dover Saturday Where He Awaits the Trial at Court.
After being chased several months by authorities of five states, Fletcher Hollis, the Smyrna negro wanted for shooting Constable James D. Wright, and for whom $250 reward was offered, was landed in Dover jail Saturday. Wright was attempting to arrest Hollis on the evening of August 3 last for disturbing a religious service, and with the assistance of Constable Charles Jones of Smyrna, apprehended the negro at the Clayton Railroad Station, when suddenly Hollis whipped out a revolver and shot Wright through the stomach, which would have killed him had it not been for a suspender button. Hollis escaped and an armed crowd searched the neighborhood of Clayton and Smyrna, threatening to burn Hollis on capture, but in vain. Hollis was caught by Washington and Baltimore authorities, but had disguised himself so completely that he was released. Finally Constable Robert Coursey, of Centreville, Md., took him and Saturday morning arraigned him before Magistrate Wood, of Dover. Hollis admitted shooting Wright, and was committed to jail in default of $2000 bail.

Hollis Had Been Shadowed for Sometime.

Constable Coursey in relating the capture to a representative of the Wilmington Sunday Star had this to say: "I had Hollis shadowed for some time before I made the arrest. Having finally perfected my plans, I secured the services and assistance of the sheriff of Queen Anne county, to go with me to the house of Hollis' aunt, where he had been stopping, and upon the best information I could secure, was there at the time I contemplated making the arrest. I had one of the officers to stay at the back door, while I entered the front door. Hollis was sitting in a chair in the room, when I greeted him with the exclamation, 'How are you Fletcher?' Hollis at once remarked, "'My name is not Fletcher Hollis." Coursey at once confronted him with the information that his name was Hollis and that he wanted him. Quick as a flash, the constable grabbed his man, as there was lying on the mantle piece a revolver with a box of cartridges beside it, and a double barreled gun. Coursey continued: "Hollis, realizing and there was no means of escape, grappled with me. I soon overpowered him and at the point of my revolver I compelled him to sit in a chair and charged him with shooting Mr. Wright. He denied it, but when I told him that the people of Clayton wanted to see him, he at once admitted everything. I handcuffed him, took him to Centreville jail and at once notified the Delaware authorities."
fletcher-hollis-smyrna-1903-08-03.A29:
HOLLIS GETS FIVE YEARS FOR SHOOTING CONSTABLE
COURT ALSO SENTENCES HIM TO STAND IN PILLORY AND PAY $500 AND COSTS.
FInal Disposition of the Exciting Case in Which the Smyrna Negro Nearly Killed Constable James D. Wright of Clayton.
Fletcher Hollis, the Smyrna negro who came near putting an end to the life of Constable James D. Wright of Clayton, by shooting him through the abdomen, was yesterday afternoon sentenced to five years' imprisonment, to stand one hour in the pillory, to pay $500 and costs of prosecution. Constable Wright, although having recovered from the effects of the wound, still carries the bullet, which has been located by the X-Rays. His life was spared because the bullet struck a button and took another course. After the shooting Hollis escaped and was a fugitive for six months, during which time he was arrested on suspicion in several cities but succeeded in making his escape every time. He was at last arrested by Constable Coursey at Centreville, Md., and landed in Dover jail. He received the full penalty of the law. Hollis first pleaded guilty in manner and form indicted and afterwards wanted to change plea that he was guilty of shooting Constable Wright, but did not intend to kill him. This, of course, could not be done and after a severe reprimand by Judge Spru- ance, he received his sentence.

PEOPLE WON'T STAND FOR MISCEGENATION
White Man and Colored Wife Driven Off by an Ohio Community.
Special to The Globe.
Special to The Globe.

SPRINGFIELD, Ohio, Oct. 7.—A few weeks ago George Guenther, white, sixty years old, married Amelia Harris, colored, thirty years old. Guenther is a wealthy farmer of Perkins. On Monday night a crowd of Perkins citizens called at the Guenther residence and informed the couple that they would have just ten days in which to get out of the country. They threatened mob law if the command was not complied with. Guenther is packing his household goods and has offered his farm for sale.
george-guenther-sandusky-1903-10-09.A2:
White Cappers.
Sandusky, Ohio, Oct. 10.—A party of a dozen masked men, armed with shotguns and revolvers, surrounded the home of George Guenther, five miles from here, at 10 o'clock last night and fairly riddled the house with bullets. Half a dozen shots struck the bed in which Guenther and his wife were lying, and one bullet struck both, but neither was badly hurt. After the fusilade had continued for some time, Guenther and his wife escaped and took refuge in the barn where they remained in their night clothes until 5:30 this morning, shivering with cold and terror. The men exhausted their ammunition before midnight, but remained about the premises until nearly daylight. The furniture in the house was riddled and 36 panes of glass were broken. This is the third attack upon the Guenthers since their marriage two weeks ago. The husband, aged 60, is white, and his wife, 30 years old, is colored. It is this mixture of races that has stirred up the neighbors.

THEY ABUSED THE FARMER
Neighbors "White-cap" a Man who Marries a Negress.
SANDUSKY, O., Oct. 10.—A sensational affair took place here last night, when George Guenther, one of the most prominent and wealthy farmers residing in this section, was white-capped and taken from his home by his neighbors, who were enraged because of the fact that he had become infatuated with and married a colored woman.

The woman Guenther married is a fine looking mulatto woman. He had been paying attention to her for some time, but his neighbors misconstrued his intentions. Suddenly, they found that he had married the woman and taken her to live at his fine new home.

Last night a number of men donned white caps, went to the house, took Guenther and his wife and dragged them out into the woods, where they maltreated them. The woman was seriously injured, and Guenther promises to make it very lively for his erstwhile friends and admirers. They, on the other hand, say they will drive him out of the country.

Guenther has hitherto traveled in the best society here.

The existing state of affairs in the department can be ascribed almost directly to the fact that since early in the McKinley administration this rule has not been observed. A Negro Killed and Seriously Wounded.

New Bern, N. C., May 5.—The Atlantic Coast Line saw fit to divide the great excursion of sixteen cars and 1,000 people in two sections last night, on account of riotous conduct. George Vann, colored, and Tom Green, white, of this city, engaged in a quarrel in the early part of the night, which led to a magistrate issuing a warrant for Vann. Officer C. Lupton recognized Vann on the excursion train and arrested him. Vann showed fight. As they got on the platform of the train, which was running six miles an hour, Vann grabbed the officer for a fight, when five shots were fired, Vann falling dead. Officer J. george-vann-newbern-1903-05-04.A6:
THE NEW BERN SHOOTING
Detailed Account of the Tragedy Aboard the Wilmington Excursion Train.
The Messenger yesterday contained a special dispatch from New Bern giving an account of the killing in that city by the police of a negro, Geo. Van, who at the time was on the excursion train bound for this city. The negro was supposed to have fatally shot a young white man named Green. Yesterday's New Bern Journal gave the following account of the affair:

"A fatal shooting occurred on board the Wilmington excursion train Monday night about 11:30 in which George Van, alias George Avant, alias 'Tuck,' a negro, was shot and instantly killed by some unknow person. The killing took place as the train had almost reached the city limits. It was caused by an attempt of the man's friends to prevent his arrest. Officer Lupton being on the train with a warrant for him. He was charged in the warrant with having shot Tom Green earlier in the night.

Van had prepared himself to resist arrest and is said to have made the boast that it would take more than one policeman to arrest him. He was surrounded and protected by his colored comrades and was ostensibly on his way to Wilmington, although he did not come with the excursionists.

"Officer Lupton was assisted by ex-Policeman Breck Dixon, who had been sworn in as deputy. They had boarded the train to look for Van, but had some trouble in locating him. After sighting him and placing him under arrest, Mr. Lupton had a severe tussle with him but had succeeded in getting him nearly out of the car when there came a fusillade of bullets. Eight or ten shots were fired and in the melee Van received a bullet in the mouth which penetrated the brain, causing instant death. At the same time Mr. Dixon was shot in the thigh. His wound is not regarded as serious.

"Unless some one confesses, the person who fired the fatal shot or who fired any of them, or whether the shooting was accidental or not will never be known, as the confusion prevented making any investigation.

"When the man fell dead train was stopped and the passengers scattered. Some jumped off the train and some went into the other car. They were a thoroughly scared bunch of people. Mr. Lupton took the dead man off the train and left the remains by the side of the track.

"Chief of Police Hargett who was in the vicinity of the train heard the shooting and hurried to the scene and seeing that the situation was critical and that a riot might occur ordered the conductor to proceed with his train. Had this not been done there might have been a general fight and a terrible tragedy taken place.

"It is important to return to the cause of the affair. As has been stated Van had been placed under arrest for shooting Tom Green. Yesterday's Journal stated that the young man was shot and seriously wounded. This was proved not to be the case, but the chief and police officers had all been led to believe that he had been shot and were looking for him until 2 o'clock Tuesday morning when he was found asleep at his boarding house. When located there he told the officers that he had started the alarm to prevent further shooting and had disappeared in order that Van could not find him as he believed he would do him harm. Had Green been found before 11:30 that night the affair might not have happened.

"Van had a character that needed sandpapering and trimming quite a good deal. He was a thoroughly bad man and had recently been released from a term in the penitentiary, having robbed a farmer of a sum of money. He had formerly lived in Wilmington but recently had been a resident of this city, but following no profession or trade.

"The coroner's jury empanelled rendered the verdict that the "deceased came to his death at the hands of person or persons unknown who were attempting to prevent his arrest."

"Officer Lupton deserves much credit for his energetic prosecution in locating and arresting a dangerous criminal. He is a good detective and a brave officer. His services should be appreciated by the citizens."

THE ASSASSIN ARRESTED. The Arrest Accomplished by the Sheriff and a Posse of Seven.
The capture of Curtis Jett, charged with the assassination of J. B. Marcum in Jackson, Ky., Monday, was accomplished without bloodshed early Sunday morning. He is now in the Clark county jail at Winchester. Bearing a warrant, which had been sworn out by Sam Jett, uncle of the accused, Sheriff McCord and a posse of seven men left Winchester at midnight Saturday. Reaching Jackson's ferry, 10 miles distant, at 2:30 a.m., they left their buggies and crossed the Kentucky river to Madison county, in canoes.

They proceeded on foot to the home of Mrs. A. Haggin, Jett's mother, two miles from the ferry. Six of the posse were stationed around the dwelling and Sheriff McCord and Deputy Stokely approached the front door and knocked. Jett's mother answered and after some parley admitted that Curtis was within. They were admitted and found Jett awake but in bed. He shook hands with the sheriff and said he would give no trouble. Reaching under his pillow he drew out his pistol and turned it over to his mother to keep. He made no show of resistance and was landed in jail at Winchester by daylight. Jett's stepfather, A. Haggin, charges that when Jett reached his house Saturday night from Jackson he proceeded to draw his pistol on him and ordered him to get out of the neighborhood. Haggin went to Richmond and swore out a warrant charging Jett with breach of the peace by assault with a pistol.

In the jail Monday Jett was communicative on all matters save the killing of Marcum. "I'll get out of this all right," was the only statement he would make which could construed as a reference to the charge. He said he wanted to be tried in Breathitt county. He was bitter in denouncing his uncle who had him arrested and said that the score would be evened up when he was at liberty. When asked about the statement that five men would testify that he killed Marcum, he sneered and said:

"What's that to you?"

To Sheriff McCord he was equally non-communicative as to the Marcum tragedy. Jett is 28 years of age, athletic in build, with deep set, keen eyes and has bushy red hair. That he submitted to arrest was an agreeable surprise to the officers, who feared an encounter. Jett denied that he drove his stepfather from home. He will be arraigned Tuesday and it is supposed he will be transferred to the Jackson district for trial.

TROOPS ARE CALLED OUT IN LOWNDES COUNTY.

THE TROUBLE.
The Officers of the Law at Hahira Had Been Defied—Several Men Were Running the Town to Their Liking—Sheriff Patterson Called Upon the Governor for Troops—No Details from Hahira, as Wires Were Not Working Late.

Atlanta, Dec. 23.—Gov. Terrell to-night received a telegram from Sheriff Patterson of Lowndes county, asking troops to suppress a riot at Hahira, twenty miles from Valdosta, where several men had defied local officers and were proceeding to run the town to their own liking.

Gov. Terrell at once wired the captain of the Valdosta Videttes to report to Sheriff Patterson, and the company will immediately leave for Hahira.

No details of the trouble are known at Valdosta, and it is impossible to reach Hahira by wire before morning.

Macon, Dec. 23.—Word from the telephone operator at Valdosta received by The Telegraph says that the Governor's message to the captain of the Valdosta military company has been delivered by courier and that the company is assembling. Trouble Between Whites and Blacks at Hahira Adjusted Itself.

Valdosta, Ga., Dec. 24.—A riot was narrowly averted at Hahira last night, and for several hours about twenty white men and as many negroes were in battle array.

It seems that a crowd of young white men had a turkey shooting in the afternoon, and a good deal of liquor was drunk about supper time, and afterwards the young men were having "Christmas fun." Some of them entered a negro restaurant and offended negroes who were there. The negroes resented it, and sides were hurriedly drawn, the entire crowd being heavily armed.

There were several knock-down and drag-out fights, and more serious trouble was imminent when Squire Lawson of the town telegraphed Sheriff Passmore for military to suppress the row. The sheriff wired Gov. Terrell but did not receive a reply until after breakfast this morning.

The sheriff and his deputy went to the scene before day this morning and returned at 7 o'clock. They found everything quiet, the trouble having blown over when the factions learned that the Valdosta Videttes were ready to rush to the scene on a minute's notice.

One of the rioters, a young white man named Pike Vickers, was arrested to-day, but was released on a bond of $150. It is said that the young white men were really responsible for the row, though they were only having fun when the trouble started.

From the facts before us it would appear that the negro's lot in the North, among the people who are supposed to love him so dearly, is even more onerous and galling than it is in the South, and the negroes' eyes are fast being opened to this fact. A dispatch from Indiana, Pa., on the 24th inst., said:

"Twenty negroes of Webrum, the entire black population of the town, were driven out yesterday after their shacks had been pulled down over their heads by the whites. White residents had given the negroes several days' notice to quit, but this, with subsequent warnings, were ignored. Yesterday a white mob gathered and, armed with ropes and poles, marched to the negro quarters Rigging the tackle on the shacks the mob tugged at the ropes and soon had the structures in ruins. After this assault the negroes hastily gathered their belonging and made for the railroad station where they boarded a freight and went to Vinton Vale, a nearby town. This is the end of the race war which broke out ten days ago."

So many cases of skin grafting occur from time to time that it is not unlikely we soon shall have human skin as an article of commerce. The perfect material is difficult to obtain. Recently a western surgeon paid $5 for sufficient pure skin to put on the limb of a child that had been badly burned. Usually relatives and friends cheerfully contribute skin for grafting, but there is no reason why healthy men and women should not sell the article. A man in sound condition might lose twenty square inches a month without suffering. In a few years he would grow an entirely new cuticle, and, perhaps, be a changed man. The prices that have been paid average about 50 cents a square inch.—New York Press.

In its anxiety to protect the sugar trust and to prevent all democratic efforts to reduce the tariff taxes, the republican party, as represented in the senate, and with the full approval of the republican president, laid aside the Cuban tariff bill, which passed the house at the first session of the fifty-seventh congress, and negotiated the Cuban reciprocity treaty now pending before the senate. DES MOINES, Aug. 24—(Special.)—One of the most unique contests ever inaugurated here marked the beginning of the actual work at the Iowa State fair today. This was the contest among farm boys of the state for a free scholarship at the State Agricultural college at Ames, based on their ability to judge stock and corn. There were twenty-four of the boys who appeared on the scene ready for work. They were placed in the judging ring of the big pavilion and shown two classes of horses and two of cattle and these were scored by all the boys, then they had two samples of corn of different varieties and these also were judged by the boys. The same animals and corn were judged by professionals at the same time and their scores reported. The scores of the farm boys will be compared with those of the professionals and the winner gets a free scholarship at the college worth $200. The contest was confined to farm boys. The following contested: Carl Freeman, Norwalk; H. Carl Schnoyer, Pocahontas; B. W. Steele, Winterset; J. B. Mitchell, Des Moines; Mark R. Barton, Roscoe; Clarence W. Robb, Newton; Lee C. Person, Sibley; Roy F. Bennett, Ames; Ellis Rail, Birmingham; Fred G. Boland, Williamsburg; Guy S. Gleason, Mechanicsville; Mereness D. Kelso, Corydon; Charles R. Stout, Stout; John Hethershaw, Des Moines; Tom S. Bell, Hancock; John H. Voder, Ware; Richard H. Stoner, South English; Harry J. Lytle, Oskaloosa; Louis J. Andrew, Morse; Marcus S. Barclay, West Liberty; Arthur Jay, Blakesburg; Andrew R. Leffer, Hillsburg; Morris J. Hester, Ames; Ralph Baldwin, Osceola. The result will not be known for several days.

Large Crowds at Start.

The attendance today was about the same as on Monday two years ago, last year being a very bad day on Monday. The railroad men report, however, that many more persons have traveled already on account of the fair than in any previous year and that they are handling large crowds for so early in the week. The program started off very well and with excellent weather. The racing commenced on the track, which was in fine condition. The stock judging commenced in the big pavilion and will commence tomorrow in the small one. The girl's orchestra from the State Industrial school furnished music at the pavilion and Reed's band from Sloux City at the races. In addition to the races there was given a series of vaudeville specialties. This evening the Pain's "Ancient Rome" was given in the race ground before a large crowd, and the fire pictures shown were those of Mrs. Roosevelt and Mrs. Cummins.

Labor Day Proclaimed.

Governor Cummins this afternoon issued a proclamation on Labor day, calling attention to the fact that this is a legal holiday in Iowa and requesting observance of the day. The governor is to speak at Colfax on Labor day.

The articles of incorporation for the Onslow Savings bank were filed with the secretary of state today, capital $10,000; C. L. Miles of Anamosa, president, and W. J. McCready, cashier. Robbers Are Very Bold.

Mrs. A. Samuels, living on Cherry street, had an exciting experience with a burglar at her home this morning. The burglar, who was a colored man, had entered the house through a window and was in the act of blowing out the night light when Mrs. Samuels was awakened. The man seized her by the throat and threatened to kill her if she made an outcry, but she made so much noise that her son in an adjoining room was awakened. The young man went outside and yelled for help and the negro made his escape at once. He dropped his hat and secured no valuables. The woman was badly frightened, but not injured. She thinks she would be able to identify the assailant.

William Harmon and John Hopper are being held under arrest in connection with the robbery of Samuel McConkey Saturday night. McConkey was quite sure that Harmon was one of the men, but both are being held until he recovers sufficiently so as to make a clear statement. He is 74 years old and may not be able to identify the men very well.

Kirby Feud Continues.

There is an interesting feud on between doctors at Grand Junction and it has broken out in court again. Last year a case was taken through the courts to make a test of certain phases of the quarantine law as related to smallpox cases, and Dr. Kirby, who violated a quarantine, was the subject of the prosecution. The supreme court found that technically Kirby was not guilty, because there was a flaw in the proceedings and the papers had not been properly signed to establish a quarantine. Now Dr. Kirby has brought suit for damages against W. B. Harker, mayor of Grand Junction, claiming $5,000 damages, because of the quarantine suit in which he was involved.

The parties placed dynamite under the full length of the house and set it off about 2 o'clock a. m. The dynamite exploded and destroyed only a part of the house; the noise was distinctly heard for miles away. About two weeks before this happened an unsuccessful attempt was made to burn the house where Chas. Richardson use to live until he moved to town. His son Elmer still lives and batches there, but was away the night the house was set on fire. The door was saturated with coal oil but the neighbors saw the blaze and put it out. The same night that they dynamited Mr. Anderson's house they tacked up the following card:

"All negroes are warned to 'git.' They are not wanted in Glive, and any white men employing them are liable to have 'something happen' to them. Section foreman employing negroes better 'fire' them at once or there will be trouble."

Then they sent unsigned letters to Ex-Representative Chas. Steward, a wealthy farmer, Mr. Olesen the Milwaukee section boss and another letter to Mr. Kirk, warning them to not hire any more colored people.

The better element of whites are indignant over this matter and they with the colored people are trying to ferret out those cowardly villains. The colored people living out there own their homes and are highly respected by their neighbors.
isaac-anderson-clive-1903-08.A12:
WHITE CAPS IN
After a laps of nearly forty years White Caps show nefarious anarchistic hand in Clive, Iowa, a suburb town of Des Moines. This time this sly sneaking monster of prejudice and hate, showed up in the form of incendiary and dynamite, attempting to destroy the homes of some colored people, giving no excuse or cause or cause at all.

The editor had an interview with several colored and white citizens living out there and they were astonished at such sneaking and cowardly acts; for those colorec citizens, less than a dozen families, are industrious, quiet peacable and law-abiding. Never has there been an arrest there since they have been out there. They all own nice homes and some very valuable land. One man advanced the idea that the cause was to threaten them so they would become dissatisfied, sell and leave the village. Whatever may be the cause the acts of those cowardly villains are more dangerous then anarchists or traitors, and if they are caught, which we hope they will be, they ought to be sent to the penitentiary for life or hung, foa this white capism, 'Tillmanism, mobism and lynching is fast speeding to the north. It must be stopped.
isaac-anderson-clive-1903-08.A15:
The Race Question.
The problem of the races is no longer confined to the South. Now it is an Iowa town where notices have been clandestinely posted ordering all the colored population to leave, and warning all residents against employing colored help in any capacity. Indiana and other northern states have communities where similar action has been, and while a race war cannot be said to be imminent, the question is assuming such proportions that it cannot be ignored.

Certainly it cannot be said that the colored race is to blame for their presence here. The first negroes were unwilling enough to be brought to these shores, and the cupidity and avarice of the whites made the inhuman institution of slavery possible. The black man is with us, because our forefathers desired him to be here, and the country must now make the best of his presence.

Violence cannot solve the problem. The colored man does not ask social recognition of the white man. It is not natural or right that the two races, distinct as they are, should mingle in social intercourse. But the negro, under our laws and the constitution, has property rights and political privileges that cannot be denied without a descent into a condition of lawlessness and anarchy.

The dominant white race has made a citizen of the black man, and it is now a public duty to make a good and efficient citizen of him. He is entitled to freedom and education, to a full understanding of our institutions, so that he can exercise his privilege of franchise intelligently. Education, not extermination nor banishment, is the solution of the race problem. It takes more than one generation to elevate an entire race from a condition of bondage to that of intelligent citizenship, and shining individual examples like Booker T. Washington show the possibilities of the colored man.

The True Northerner believes in an intelligent citizenship, and would have no fault with the establishment of a uniform standard for black and white alike, throughout the land, which it would be necessary for every man to attain before he should have the right to a voice at the ballot box.

The crimes to which negroes as a race seem inclined, and which are responsible for the horrid record of lynchings in this country, particularly in the South, are but the natural result of ignorance, the sure harvest of centuries when the race knew no law but the whip of the tyrannical master.

Each state owes free, patriotic education to every one of its children, white or black, and we believe no dangers are to be feared from an intelligent citizenship, whatever its color may be.

Lawlessness has no legitimate place in our system of government, whether directed against the individual or a race, and a wholesome regard of law is a crying demand of the times. And nothing could do more to bring it about than an honest effort to bring every violator of the law to justice, and that speedily.

The law's delay is responsible for many resorts to the court of Judge Lynch and the jury of the mob.
isaac-anderson-clive-1903-08.A20:
ORDERED TO VACATE.
Colored Man at Clive Causes Indignation Among Citizens.
Des Moines, Ia., Aug. 25.—After a futile effort to dynamite the barn and home of I. Anderson, a colored man residing at Clive, a small town on the Milwaukee, six miles west of Des Moines, supposed White Caps have pasted notices in conspicuous places warning the colored population to flee, and threatening all white men who employ colored help or in any way assist the colored residents of that burg. The posting of the notices has strenger terror to the hearts of the threatened, and it is feared trouble may result.

isaac-jones-tarrytown-1903-01-10.A2:
NEGRO TRIES ASSAULT.
Young Woman of Pocantico Hills Rescued by Police Officer.
Mamie Foley, twenty-one years old, a daughter of Michael Foley, a citizen of Pocantico Hills, Westchester County, the country home of John D. Rockefeller, was held up late Saturday night in Tarrytown by a negro named Isaac Jones, who attempted to assault her. Miss Foley was walking in a lonely part of the city, near the railroad tracks, when Jones met her and seized her by the throat. He quickly overpowered her and dragged her through a vacant lot to a shed.

Her screams were heard by Officer Burns, who ran to the place. When he arrived he saw the man running away. Burns gave chase, and after a hard run caught the negro just as he was going into a saloon. He overpowered the man and took him to the police station. Jones was held for the grand jury on a charge of attempted assault, and was hurried to White Plains before the crime became generally known.

Jones drives a coal wagon for Dinkel, Jewell & Co. He is married and has three children.
isaac-jones-tarrytown-1903-01-10.A4:
NEGRO TRIES ASSAULT.
Former Rockefeller Servant Charged with the Crime.
The people of Tarrytown-on-the-Hudson are aroused over the acts of several negroes who have attacked women in the streets lately, and it is feared there will be trouble. James Hill, a colored man, formerly in the employ of William Rockefeller, held up Mrs. Louis Wall, in Central-ave. Tarrytown, on Tuesday night, and tried to assault her, it is alleged.

She fought the negro off, and her screams for help brought Policeman Henry Palmer, who attacked the woman's assailant. The negro drew a revolver and fired four times at the policeman at close range, but the shots went wild, and the officer managed to arrest him after he had been knocked down.

This made the second attack of a negro on women in Tarrytown in the last three days. On Saturday night a mob of two hundred people went to the village jail to lynch Isaac Jones, a colored fellow who had, it is alleged, attempted to assault a young white girl named Foley. The members of the mob were armed with clubs and carried ropes. They declared they would string up the prisoner to a telegraph pole. The police played a clever ruse, declaring that the negro had been taken to the county jail, and the crowd dispersed.

THREE HURT IN TRAIN CRASH. Passenger and Railroad Men, Victims of Wreck on New York Central, Will Probably Die. SCHENECTADY. N. Four Years for Negro Brute.
(Special to The Evening World.)

WHITE PLAINS, April 2.—Isaac Jones, a negro, who was nearly lynched in Tarrytown several months ago for attacking Miss Annie Foley, was sentenced by County Judge Platt at White Plains to-day to four years and six months at hard labor in Sing Sing prison. "You are a brute of the worst kind," said the Judge in passing sentence.

james-nelson-jefferson-1903-11-21.A1:
LIFE THE PENALTY
A NEGRO BRUTE PAID TO LYNCHERS FOR HIS ATTEMPT
UPON A LITTLE WHITE GIRL.
CHESTERFIELD COUNTY HAD ITS FIRST LYNCHING.
South Carolina Mob Took a 19-Year-Old Negro from His Captors—Silently They Strung Him Up—Not a Shot Was Fired, and Neighbors Did Not Know of the Lynching Until Next Day—Body Left Hanging for the Coroner.

Columbia, S. C., Nov. 23.—News reached here late to night of the lynching of James Nelson, a negro, near Jefferson, Chesterfield county, Saturday night. Chesterfield county has heretofore been clear of lynching, and the illegal hanging Saturday night is the second execution to occur within her borders in almost a half century.

On Saturday afternoon, Nov. 15, an attempt was made to outrage the 7-year-old daughter of Miles W. Porter, a prominent farmer of the upper part of Chesterfield county, by Jim Nelson, a negro laborer, employed on Mr. Porter's farm.

The girl and some smaller children were playing at a spring near the house when the attempt was made. They ran to the house and gave the alarm. The purpose of the brute was not accomplished.

Pursuit Was Organized.

The negro took to the woods, and early Monday morning a posse was organized and for several days scoured the woods and nearby swamps in search of him, but without success. The father and brothers of the child continued to hunt, and Saturday afternoon Mr. Will Porter came upon him at Maynard's sawmill, near Catarrh. He carried him to Jefferson and placed him in the guard house in the afternoon, and about 8 o'clock Saturday night Mr. Porter and Mr. E. G. Ingram started with the negro to Chesterfield to deliver him to the sheriff.

When about three miles from Jefferson a couple of men appeared from out of the woods, presented revolvers and ordered the men in the buggy to hold up their hands, which command was promptly obeyed. They were then ordered to drive on for about 100 yards up the road. The negro was dragged from the buggy and Ingram and Porter were ordered to turn about and drive away.

About twenty or thirty men on horseback were congregated about this lonely spot and made quick work of their victim. A rope was placed around his neck, and he was swung up and left hanging, while the knights of the cord rode silently away into the darkness.

Crowds Saw the Body.

Nelson's body was left hanging all day Sunday, and hundreds of people went to look upon it. He was black, about 19 years old, with thick lips and shaggy hair. Not a shot was fired, and a family living within 200 yards of the scene did not know until Sunday morning the meaning of the presence of the silent horsemen, who passed and repassed in the moon light of the night before.

The coroner went to the scene of the lynching Sunday evening, and empanelled a jury, and by the light of pine knots held the inquest over the dead body. The verdict was that Jim Nelson had met his death at the violent hands of parties unknown to the jury.

The body was buried near the road, no relatives having come to claim it.
james-nelson-jefferson-1903-11-21.A2:
Lynching at Jefferson, S. C.
Columbia, S. C., Nov. 24.—A report has reached here that James Nelson, a negro charged with attempted assault on a white girl, has been lynched near Jefferson, S. C.

Attest.

Negroe's Body Swung to Limb By Silent Horsemen.

Silent Horsemen.

Chesterfield county has heretofore been clear of lynchings and the illegal hangings is the second execution to occur within her borders in almost a half century.

He carried him to Jefferson and placed him in the guard house in the afternoon, and about 8:30 that night Mr. Porter and E. G. Ingram started with the negro to Chesterfield to deliver him to the sheriff.

The news that he had been captured had circulated around and a posse was quickly made up, the two gentlemen were met on the road the negro was taken from them and swung to a nearby tree and riddled with bullets.
james-nelson-jefferson-1903-11-21.A4:
Lynching In Chesterfield
The Usual Crime the Cause--Silent Horsemen Came in the Moonlight and Did Their Work.
Special to The State.
Chesterfield, Nov. 23.—News reached here this morning of the lynching of Jim Nelson, a coal black negro, near Jefferson, this county, Saturday night. The news was received here very quietly and elicited little comment on the streets. Chesterfield county has heretofore been clear of this kind of lynching and the illegal hanging of Saturday night is the second execution to occur within her borders in almost a half century. Your correspondent went to the scene of the crime and is enabled to give the facts of the whole matter.

On Saturday afternoon, Nov. 15, an attempt was made to outrage the 7-year old daughter of Miles W. Porter, a prominent farmer of the upper part of Chesterfield county, by Jim Nelson, a negro laborer employed on Mr. Porter's farm.

The girl and some smaller children were playing at a spring near the house when the attempt was made. They ran to the house and gave the alarm and the purpose of the brute was not accomplished. The negro took to the woods and early Monday morning a posse was organized and for several days scoured the woods and nearby swamps in search of him, but without success. The father and brothers of the child continued the hunt and Saturday afternoon Mr. Will Porter came up with the negro at Maynard's saw mill near Catarrh. He carried him to Jefferson and placed him in the guard house in the afternoon, and about 8:30 o'clock Saturday night Mr. Porter and Mr. E. G. Ingram started with the negro to Chesterfield to deliver him to the sheriff. When about three miles from Jefferson a couple of men appeared from out of the woods, presented revolvers and ordered the men in the buggy to hold up their hands, which command was promptly obeyed. They were then ordered to drive on for about 200 yards, where a good healthy limb of a large blackjack hung invitingly over the road and the negro was dragged from the buggy and Ingram and Porter were ordered to turn about and drive for what they were worth. About 20 or 30 men on horseback were congregated at this lonely spot and made quick work of their victim. A rope was placed around his neck and he was swung up and left hanging, while the knights of the cord rode silently away into the darkness.
james-nelson-jefferson-1903-11-21.A12:
STATE NEWS.
Governor Heyward is being beigeged by people who want pardous for convicts.

— Robert A. Law, of Spartanburg, has won the Townsend scholarship in Harvard college.

— Col. S. T. Poiner's appointment as postmaster of Spartanburg was confirmed in the Senate without a dissenting vote.

— The Atlantic Coast Line Railway is going to provide for pensions for old and infirm employees worn out in their service.

— About sixteen thousand bales of cotton have already been sold in Newberry this season. The receipts there this year have been better than for several years past.

— Jessie Henderson, who killed Jonas Hammond in a church row near Johnston some months ago, was arrested in Waynesboro, Ga., and brought to Edgefield last week.

— While a chaingang was at work grading drives in Hampton Park, Charleston, a huge cannon ball was unearthed supposed to have been fired from Morris Island during the Civil war.

— Mrs. I. G. McKissick will endow a library room in the Connie Maxwell orphanage, Greenwood, in memory of her son, Ed. P. McKissick, late proprietor of Battery Park hotel, Asheville.

— President Roosevelt has re-appointed Rev. Joshua E. Wilson, colored, postmaster at Florence against an almost unanimous protest of the business men and other patrons of the office there.

Governor Heyward and Major Micah Jenkins went to Washington recently to see the president and the secretary of war relative to locating an army post in Columbia and received encouragement to expect it.

Hamp Jones, the negro under sentence to be hanged at Marion, will not die on the gallows. Sheriff Mullins has at last been officially notified of the fact that Gov Heyward has commuted the sentence to life imprisonment.

On the charge of arson two young white men, Broadus and Lannie Lollia, sons of Jack Lollia, a somewhat noted horse trader of Laurens county, have been arrested and committed to jail on the charge of burning the residence of Mrs. Eden Owens, a neighbor to the Lollises.

About 100,000 acres in Richland county are not on the county auditor's books, according to the returns made and the official map used. Two large distilleries were captured by the United States Revenue officers in Oconee County last week and destroyed. One of the plants destroyed, is said to be the largest still ever destroyed in South Carolina. It consisted of a ninety-gallon copper still, cap and worm, thirty-one fermenters, and 3,500 gallons of beer. The second plant destroyed had only seven fermenters and 400 gallons of mash.

Rev. W. G. Neville, of York county, has a novel plan for raising church money. Last spring he distributed sixty quarts of cottonseed to members of his congregation who promised to turn the cotton produced over to the church. He called for the delivery of the cotton and had it ginned. They, met had a big pionic dinner and ascertained that they had a bale of cotton weighing 500 pounds.

jess-bruce-red-oak-1903-09-11.A1:
SHOT INTO HOUSE.
Attempt .Made to Assassinate Negro Cotton Pickers.
Waxahachie, Tex., Sept. 10.—At a late hour Wednesday night an unknown party fired a volley of shots into a negro cabin on the farm of J. T. Sullivan near Red Oak. Two occupants of the cabin, George Hill and Jess Bruce, were wounded, but not seriously. Hill was shot in the left shoulder with a pistol. Bruce received a charge of shot in one arm. The negroes were there picking cotton.
jess-bruce-red-oak-1903-09-11.A2:
Attack on Negro Cotton Pickers.
Houston, Texas, Sept. 11.—Negro cotton pickers, sleeping in a house near Red Oak were fired on early this morning by unknown parties. Fifty shots were fired. Two men were killed and two women wounded.
jess-bruce-red-oak-1903-09-11.A3:
NEGROES
Killed by Unknown Assassins in Texas.
Scripps-McRae Telegram.

Scripps-McRae Telegram. Houston, Tex., Sept. 11.—Negro cotton pickers who were sleeping in a hut near Red Oak were fired on early this morning by unknown parties. Fifty shots were fired. Two men were killed and two women wounded. There is no clew to the assailants.

jim-pruitt-1903-05-26.A1: Jim Pruitt, colored, living in the Cross Anchor section of Spartan bug, went to Spartanburg last week and appeared before Magistrate Kirby with a pitiful tale—how some white men several days before had taken him from his home and administered a severe beating. The case will be investigated. The negro could assign no cause for such punishment.
jim-pruitt-1903-05-26.A2:
Whipped by White Caps.
A Spartanburg dispatch to The State says Thursday afternoon Jim Pruitt, colored, accompanied by his wife, Alma Pruitt, from the Cross Anchor section, arrived in the city and appeared at Magistrate Kirby's office. They released a pitiful tale of misery—how some white men had taken Jim Pruitt from his house last Tuesday night and administered on his bare limbs a severe whipping; so lacerating and bruising him that he was scarcely able to walk. It appears, however, that he made out t journey to that city one week later. He was certainly well flogged. Neither Jim nor his wife seem to know why the men whipped him. The white cappers threatened them with death if they made any mention of the lawless occurrence. Magistrate Kirby referred them, by letter, to Magistrate Mike Patton, at Cross Anchor, who will doubtless investigate the case and put an end to such proceedings.

Four Killed.

Four men killed and two badly burned by an explosion of gas in the mines of the Chartres Coal and Coke company at Federal, a mining town near Bridgeville on the Pittsburg, Chartres and Youghiogheny railroad Tuesday. The mine is but slightly injured.

Acquitted.

Mrs. Eile L. Carson, who shot and killed Robert Rigsby in Macon, Ga., some months ago for making slanderous remarks about her, has been acquitted. When the verdict of the jury was announced there was considerable applause.

The Fitzgerald Enterprise says: "P-r-e-c-e-d-e-n-t is what stands between Grover and a third term." Whereupon The Hawkinsville Dispatch and News sagely remarks: "Call it precedent if you want to, but the correct word is 'voters.'"

joe-hallier-horse-creek-1903-08-10.A1:
LABOR LEADERS MOBBED
UNUSUAL CASE OF ASSAULT IN ALA-BAMA MINE DISTRICT.
One of the Men Is a Negro, and the Fact that They Worked Together Caused the Maltreatment.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., Aug. 11.—Joe Hallier, a district organizer of the United Mine Workers of America, was shot and seriously wounded in the arm at Horse Creek yesterday morning and B. L. Greer, colored, vice president of the Alabama United Mine Workers, was assaulted and severely beaten by a crowd of angry citizens.

Mr. Hallier had been to Empire with Vice President Greer, where a small local of the United Mine Workers was organized, and the two men were about to take the train for Birmingham. According to the account of Greer they were in the depot when five men entered and at the point of pistols ordered the two men to march down the railroad track. They started and were then ordered to trot, which they also did. Various indignities were heaped upon them, Mr. Hallier being forced to kiss Greer. Greer was then assaulted and beaten until the blood flowed profusely.

While Mr. Hallier was being forced to trot the men began firing at him and he finally fell. The pursuers then left him and returned to town. The two men were picked up by a freight train.
joe-hallier-horse-creek-1903-08-10.A3:
THE COMPANY STORES
COMMISSIONARY SYSTEM BEFORE THE ARBITERS.
Many Prominent Citizens Are Attentive Auditors—Miners Conclude Their Evidence Inside the Time Allowed Them.
Birmingham, Aug. 11.—(Special.)—The attendance at the second day's sitting of the Board of Arbitration, which is to decide the differences between operators and miners in this State, was larger than on yesterday. Many prominent citizens of Birmingham and the northern part of the State are present and are watching the proceedings. General Benjamin F. Tracy of New York, is a close observer. Don. H. Bacon, President of the Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company, was present this morning and was also a close listener. Most of the testimony adduced today was in reference to the company stores or commissary, the Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company stores at Pratt City, Ensley and Wylam being discussed. The check system was thoroughly threshed over. Adam Pow, 14 years a miner in Alabama, with a family of eleven children, all of whom are receiving a college education, was on the stand. He told of the operations of the stores. He himself took up no checks from the company, but bought them on the outside. He said that when he paid cash for his goods in the stores he got them at 15 per cent discount. He knew of regularly hired agents who bought and sold these checks, the object being to swell the store receipts.

Patrick Barrett of Wylam was on the stand and told of store operations also.

Both of these witnesses do extra work in the mines, the first attending to narrow work, making as high as $80 per month, and the other being a pillar puller and receiving $60 per month. Both testified to a surplus of men at some of the mines. Pow stated that on the second or third day of each month the company issued the store checks and that just as many men stopped off work as did on the day that money was paid out.

The witnesses are being cross-examined closely by the attorneys for the operators. The miners announced that they had but few witnesses to introduce and offered the annual reports of several of the companies in this district showing profits on coal, coke, iron and stores, as to the claim of the miners for an advance of 5 cents per ton. The miners also offered the official proceedings of the joint conference between the operators and miners in June and July when efforts were made to get a contract, giving figures from the operators' side as to iron, coal and coke prices. This was offered in substantiation of the demand for 5 cents per ton advance in prices.

The attorneys for the operators offered objection on the grounds that the figures quoted then and statements made then were for the purpose of effecting a compromise. Judge Gray decided that the proceedings could be presented but of course would be acted upon as the arbiters saw fit. The miners finished inside their allotted time. President Ed. Flynn of the district organization of the miners, is prosecuting the case and he is doing well.

According to the plans, the operators have five days in which to present their answers and evidence. In admitting what other witnesses would swear to in reference to commissary or store checks, the attorneys for the operators announced that when their time came they would show that the companies made no money on the buying and reselling of the checks or in giving discount to the outside customers, except in the legitimate operation of the store.

W. R. Fairley and T. L. Lewis, members of the board of arbitration, and members of the United Mine Workers of America, asked witnesses today many questions, as did Judge Gray.

At the afternoon session of the board of arbitration L. B. Evans testified as to the commissary at Graves Mines operated by the Lacey Buek Company. He said the company issued a check each day and men who wanted cash before the regular pay day discounted these check at 25 per cent. He also said goods in the Graves store were higher than in the city stores.

The miners announced that they would offer no other witnesses, but would press the objection made as to several matters brought up by the operators for arbitration.

There was much argument on this matter.

The board will render its decision on this subject tomorrow morning. J. W. McQueen, second vice-president of the Sloss-Sheffield Steel and Iron Company, was the first witness put on by the operators. He said his company ran about eight stores and they sold goods fresher and cheaper than other stores. He said his company does not buy checks from its miners. He gave some figures as to miners' earnings in the mines. He was still on the stand when adjournment was taken until tomorrow.

Organizers Roughly Treated.

At Horse Creek, Walker County, today Joe Hollier, white, district organizer, and Ben L. Greer, colored, district vice-president of the United Mine Works of America, were roughly treated by a posse of white men. The two union men were organizing locals.

Last night they organized a small local at Empire, nine miles from Horse Creek. They stopped at the latter place en route to Birmingham. At the depot they were approached by several white men and Greer was beat on the head then Hollier was approached and he knocked down the assuperintendent of the place.

At the points of pistols the two men were forced to leave the place. On the road uot of town Hollier was compelled to kiss Greer and other more horrible doings were suggested by the posse. Then Hollier and Greer were forced to run and the posse fired on them. Hollier was struck in the arm, an artery being severed. He almost died from loss of blood. He was brought to Birmingham on a litter and is now at an infirmary. His condition is serious.

Horse Creek is a non-union mining camp. Greer claims that the men who assaulted him and Hollier were not miners.

There was great indignation expressed over the occurrence by the citizens. Sheriff Frank Moore and a posse of deputies went from Jasper to Horse Creek
joe-hallier-horse-creek-1903-08-10.A4:
JOE HALLIER IS SERIOUSLY SHOT

District Organizer of Miners
Pursued by Crowd
INDIGNITIES WERE HEAPED
Hallier and Vice President Greer, Colored, Had Organized Miners' Local at Empire—The Shooting Was at Horse Creek.
Joe Hallier, Alabama district organizer of the United Mine Workers of America, was shot and seriously wounded in the arm at Horse Creek yesterday morning, and B. L. Greer, colored, vice president of the Alabama United Mine Workers, was assaulted and severely beaten by a crowd of angry citizens.

Mr. Hallier was wounded in the left arm, the bullet entering at the back of the upper arm and coming out in front. An artery was severed and he was brought to the city on a freight train and carried to the Copeland & Berry infirmary, where an operation was performed to close the artery.

Heaping Indignities.

He had been to Empire, a small settlement near Horse Creek, with Vice President Greer, where a small local of the United Mine Workers was organized, and the two men had come to Horse Creek to take the train for Birmingham.

According to the account of Greer they were in the depot when five men entered, headed by Charles Moore, superintendent of the Ivy Leaf mines, and they were ordered to march down the railroad track at the point of pistols. They started, and were then ordered to trot, which they also did. Various indignities were heaped upon them, Mr. Hallier being forced to kiss Greer. Greer was assaulted and beaten so that the blood flowed profusely.

While Mr. Hallier was being forced to trot, the men began firing at him and he finally fell with the wound in his arm. The pursuers then left him and returned to the town. Greer stayed with him and they were picked up by a crew of a freight train which passed soon and brought to Birmingham.

It is alleged that an official of one of the mining companies led the crowd. It is also said that there was a justice of the peace in the crowd.

Mr. Hallier was unable to talk last night and he was still under the influence of the anaesthetic which had been given him.

His Assailants Given Preliminary Trial Yesterday FIVE WITNESSES TESTIFY
Question of Citizenship of the Complaining Witness Was Raised By A. D. Smith, Counsel for the Defense.
The most interesting point raised at the preliminary hearing of the six Walker county men charged with conspiracy against District Organizer Joe Hallier of the United Mine Workers of America, which was heard before United States Commissioner Wilson yesterday, was whether Mr. Hallier is a legally naturalized citizen of the United States or not.

Hallier was born in Wales and came to this country when 19 years of age. His father had been here for several years before the coming of the son. Upon reaching his majority Mr. Hallier declared his intention of becoming a citizen before a justice of the peace in Blocton. That was about twelve years ago. During the past few years, however, he has enjoyed all the privileges and rights of an American citizen. He has voted regularly in the state. He does not know whether his father was legally naturalized or not.

The Defense.

The counsel for the defense contended yesterday that he is not a citizen in the eyes of the law and is not entitled to have a suit brought in his behalf in the courts of this country.

The commissioner ruled, however, that the hearing of evidence should be proceeded with. In all five witnesses were examined during the day.

The defendants in the cause are Charley Moore, William Ballinger, John Chance, James E. DeLoach, R. B. Patton and Steve Smith. All the defendants had been previously arrested with the exception of Moore and Smith and were out on $2,000 bond. Moore and Smith appeared in the court room yesterday voluntarily. They are charged with conspiracy to deprive Joe Hallier of certain rights guaranteed to him by the constitution and laws of the United States. According to the testimony Mr. Hallier and B. L. Greer, vice president of the district organization of the mine wrkers, went to Empire, in Walker county to organize a local union on the night of August 10th. On the morning of the 11th, while they were waiting at Horse Creek for a train to Birmingham, they were assaulted and offered certain indignities and Mr. Hallier was shot in the arm.

It is alleged that the assailants represented the non-union miners of Walker county and that their action grew out of a determination not to allow the United Mine Workers to get a footing in the county.

Legal Talent.

The prosecution is being conducted by United States District Attorney T. R. Roulhac, assisted by Assistant Attorneys W. H. Standifer and N. L. Steele and Vaughan & Davidson and Lee Cowart. The defendants were represented by John J. Moore, A. D. Smith and E. D. Smith.

At the beginning of the hearing, which was held in the United States court room, the rule was called for and all the witnesses except Joe Hallier and B. L. Greer left the room. A. D. Smith announced that the defense did not think the federal court had jurisdiction in the matter and asked permission to make demurrer to the complaint. Judge Roulhac stated that that was satisfactory and that the taking of testimony could be proceeded with.

Hallier on the Stand.

Joe Hallier was the first witness placed upon the stand. He testified that he resided at Blocton; that he supposed he was a citizen of the United States; that he was at Horse Creek on August 11, arriving there from Empire at about 8:55; that he had organized a local of the U. M. W. of A. at Empire on the night before and that B. L. Greer was with him. He said that he had been informed that he could get a train to Birmingham in thirty minutes, but that the station agent told him there was not one until three in the afternoon, and that he then went on the platform to tell Greer about it. Proceeding he said:

"Greer said that he was hungry and would like to have some breakfast. About that time I saw four or five men coming down the road from the direction of Cordova and when about twenty feet from me one of them beckoned to me. He asked me if my business was not organizing local miners union and if the negro did not belong with me. He then cursed me telling me to get away from him and struck at me with his fist. I ducked and he missed me, but fell down and as he rolled sideways he pulled a gun.

Guns Pointed at Him.

"As I straightened up guns were pointed at me on all sides. Charley Moore was the man that struck the blow."

The witness here identified James De Loach and R. B. Patton as two of the men who were with Moore. The defendants were seated just inside the rail. Continuing the witness said:

"Greer said something and Mr. Moore started toward him. One man struck at me with a gun and I grabbed it. The others were hammering Greer over the head with their guns. Finally I loosed my hold and went toward Greer who was bleeding profusely. Moore then ordered us to go up the track. He is the man who did most of the talking. I started down the dirt road and he ordered me on the railroad. About 75 yards down the track Moore ordered me to kiss the negro and as he had his gun pointed at me I had to obey.

The witness then said Moore said that a little later he would make him undergo an unnameable indignity. Mr. Hallier continued:
