LITTLE CRIMINALS AGAIN IN TROUBLE
TWO NEGRO BOYS SCARCELY OUT OF BABYHOOD ARRESTED ON A CHARGE OF STEALING CHICKENS-WONDERFULLY AGILE.
Two of the members of the infant gang of negro criminals of Birmingham are again in the hands of the police.

The little negroes are Luther Daniels and Dennis Seyers, neither of whom are much more than babies, but both are often in trouble on one charge or another.

This time there are two charges of larceny against each of them, and naturally one of the charges is for stealing chickens. If there are two negroes who are more successful in stealing chickens than any other two negroes in Birmingham it is this pair. They are so small that they can crawl into a hole much less than a foot square, and they can skin out to the very end of the small limbs of trees to get the fowls where they roost.

For the past four years this gang has done everything in the criminal line that boys could do, and it has even been thought once or twice that they were connected with several large burglaries, which were committed, but no evidence against them could ever be obtained.

When there are any petty crimes committed and the police have cause to believe young negroes committed them, the first specimens looked for are Luther Daniels and his gang. They are generally easily found, but never easily caught, as they can run like rabbits. It is a peculiar fact that there are never any petty crimes committed by young negroes when Luther and the other subleaders of the gang are in jail, but as soon as they get out something happens.

The members of this gang have spent fully four-fifths of their time in the city jail, and the police regard them as the future bad criminals of Birmingham.

As to Greer.
The commissioner ruled yesterday that the name of Greer could be inserted. When he announced that the defendants were released many in the court room were visibly surprised, but there was much congratulation among the defendants and their friends. The commissioner stated that his decision was based on the fact that it had not been proved by the evidence that Hallier was naturalized. He said that while he would allow the name of Greer, who has lived in Alabama all his life, to be inserted in the affidavit he did not think that the evidence brought out at the preliminary was sufficient to hold the defendants for a conspiracy against Greer. He also stated that if Hallier had been shown to be naturalized he would have bound the defendants over on the evidence.

The matter has attracted considerable attention, especially among the miners and operators of the district. Charley Moore, William Ballenger, James E. Deoach, John Chance, R. B. Patton and Steve Smith of Walker county, were charged with having made an assault on Hallier and Greer at Horse Creek on August 11. The evidence showed that these two men had been driven from town, beaten, kicked, humiliated and fired upon, one shot striking Hallier in the right arm.

Cause of Trouble.

This attack was said to have been made because Hallier and Greer had organized a local union of the miners at Empire on the previous night, the assailants being in sympathy with the non-union miners, and one of them having said that they did not propose to let the United Mine Workers come over in Walker county and run their business.

The action taken by Commissioner Wilson does not prevent the matter from coming before the federal grand jury when it next sits. The defendants had been under $2000 bond each until yesterday.

FROM U. S. COURT
Judge Jones Hands Down an Important Decision
THE ASSAULTING OF GREER
Alleged Conspiracy to Prevent United Mine Workers to Organize In Walker County a State Court Matter.
Judge Thomas G. Jones, of the United States court, has handed down a decision dismissing the case of the United States against Charles Moore, William Ballinger, John Chance, George DeLoach, Luther Rayburn and Sterling Shores, indicted by the federal grand jury on two counts under section No. 5508 of the Revised Statutes. In the first count of the indictments it was charged that the defendants conspired to injure, oppress and intimidate one B. L. Greer, a citizen of the United States, to prevent the free exercise and enjoyment by him by the constitution or laws of the United States, to wit: "The right and privilege of establishing and organizing a local union of the United Mine Workers or America in the county of Walker, and state of Alabama," and that the defendants "unlawfully assaulted and beat the said Greer," while the second count of the indictments charged that to effect the objects of the conspiracy formed by the defendants that Greer was assaulted with an intent to murder.

The order of Judge Jones thus expunges from the federal courts two important cases sent up from Walker county. The basis of the cases was an alleged assault upon Joe Hallier, district organizer, and B. L. Greer, colored, vice president of District No. 20, United Mine Workers of America, near Horse Creek, last summer, where they had gone presumably for the purpose of organizing unions among the miners. The Hallier case was dismissed because it was not conclusively shown at the preliminary trial before a United States commissioner that he was a naturalized citizen of the United States. In rendering the decree, the demurrers of the attorneys for the defendants, Walker Percy and W. I. Grubbs, to the indictments are sustained by the court.

Grounds for Demurrer.

Substantially the grounds for the demurrers were as follows:

"1. Because it appears from the indictment that the right or privilege claimed is not secured to said Greer as a citizen of the United States by the constitution
"2. Because the indictment shows that no offense was committed against the criminal laws of the United States, but only an offense against the laws of the state of Alabama.

"3. The indictment shows that this court has no jurisdiction to try and punish the offense set forth."

In the preface of Judge Jones' decision is the following:

"Unquestionably the right of a citizen to organize miners, artisans, laborers or persons in any pursuit, as well as the right of individuals in such callings to unite for their own improvement and advancement, or for any other lawful purpose, is a fundamental right of a citizen, protected in every free government worthy of the name. The only issue this case presents is, to what government, under our complex institutions, is committed the duty to protect that right?"
"To ascertain the privileges and immunities of citizens of the United States, and the rights which pertain to the citizens of the state as such, we must consult the history of our institutions, as well as the history of the constitution, says the opinion. "It is quite apparent that as to a great number of matters the citizen must still look to the states to protect him in the enjoyment of life, liberty, property and the pursuit of happiness.

Negro Saved From Lynching.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 21.—John Jackson, a negro, was nearly lynched near Many, Sabine Point, La., for assault on the wife of Harry Mason at Zwolle, a small town on the Kansas City Southern Railroad. Mrs. Mason was badly injured in her struggle with the negro. Jackson was captured shortly afterward and taken before Mrs. Mason and identified. An attempt was made to lynch him at Zwolle, but the constable succeeded in getting him to the parish prison.

COLORED BELL BOY ATTACKED AND CRUELLY BEATEN. Attack Made in Pure Maliciousness by Three Men, Who Escaped Arrest.
John Logan, a colored bellboy employed at the Oneida Hotel, had an unpleasant experience with "Bungaloos" last night. His brief experience with the "Bungaloos" resulted in his carrying a cut lip to the City Dispensary, where three stitches were sewn in it and the injured part of his face soothed somewhat by lotions. Logan lives at 321 Ellsworth street. He has a story of trouble that could only be told to a policeman, and were told to Sergeant Warren at police headquarters last night.

Logan was riding his bicycle around Monument place about 9 o'clock and as he is very black and conspicuous by his color he attracted attention and several white men who were under the influence of liquor and passing around the monument more or less noisily called him "nigger, nigger," and tried to stop him in order that one of them, more abusive than the rest, might do as he offered to do—"Knock his block off." Logan didn't accept the invitation and instead continued on his way until he met Patrolmen Dolby and Gregory, and asked their assistance in punishing the men. Dolby and Gregory searched for the men with Logan, but could not find them. They told Logan to stand on the sidewalk in front of the Postal Telegraph office on South Meridian street until the men appeared and then attract their attention. After the men attacked him, as the patrolmen promised they would, he was to run to the entrance to Pearl street with the men pursuing him. The patrolmen promised to wait for him and to arrest the men when he got them into an alley.

Logan waited until the men appeared and then played decoy. He was a decoy. One of the men hit him in the mouth and the other knocked him down. Logan could not run and his mouth was so full of blood that he couldn't cry out. When he did get up he found that the policemen had left him a victim to the three men who attacked him, beat him and went on their way rejoicing.

Logan telephoned, as he said, for the "bike cops," but the police were unable to find his assailants.
john-logan-indianapolis-1903-04-28.A3:
AFTER BUNGALOO GANG BOARD OF SAFETY DIRECTED TO MAKE AN INVESTIGATION. Patrolmen Dolby and Gregory Will Make Explanation-Other Municipal Affairs.
Mayor Bookwalter yesterday directed the Board of Public Safety to make a thorough investigation of the charge that Patrolmen Dolby and Gregory had used John Logan, a colored boy, as a decoy to capture some of the rowdies known as the "bungaloos" and had failed to protect Logan. Logan at first said the patrolmen induced him to lead the rowdies, who take delight in overpowering negroes and beating them, into Pearl street, where they promised to be in hiding. Logan carried out his part of the programme and he was badly beaten. The board at its session yesterday decided to make a complete investigation, and Superintendent Taffe was instructed to bring the witnesses before the board.

Mayor Bookwalter said last night: "I want to know if such a situation existed. If patrolmen make such arrangements they must carry them out. I have given instructions that this bungaloo business must be broken up. If it is necessary the day force will be ordered out in citizens' clothes to apprehend these villains."

Superintended Taffe says the police have tried numerous schemes to catch the bungaloo ringleaders but without success. Colored men disguised have sought the places where this crowd usually congregates and invited assault in order that patrolmen in citizens' clothes could capture them. But the rowdies did not appear. The headquarters now seems to be South Illinois street and an extra force will be put on in this district to prevent further disturbances.

DID NOT NEGLECT DUTY.

The impression created by the story of the assault on John Logah, colored, by three unknown white men Tuesday night on South Meridian street, printed in the Journal yesterday morning, that Patrolmen Gregory and Dolby were neglectful of their care of Logan is an erroneous one. The young man appealed to the policemen for assistance, and they spent one hour and twenty minutes with him in searching for the men. They endeavored to locate the men by posting themselves at Pearl and Meridian streets while Logan waited in front of the offices of the Postal Telegraph Company. After a wait of some time the negro went to the police, and the three agreed that the men would not return, and the patrolmen advised the boy to go to his home. After that the policemen left the boy and proceeded to make a trip around their district.

After Dolby and Gregory had gone, Logan stood around talking to messenger boys in front of the telegraph office, and the men who had accosted him on Monument place appeared. One of the men struck him in the mouth, but did not knock him down, he says. His bicycle was punctured by one of them in a spirit of maliciousness, and, after assaulting him, the men walked on and he was left to secure care for his damaged mouth and to notify the police station, where he reported the occurrence.

The police have secured from Logan a written statement that they were with him for an hour and twenty minutes, and the boy so stated to a reporter last night. The boy said at the police station it was not the fault of the police that he was beaten by the bungaloos, and it was not understood that way at the police station when the report was made.

GIRL'S BODY IS FOUND
VICTIM OF AN UNKNOWN NEGRO'S CRIME NEAR LAWRENCEBURG.
She Was Not Ravished by Her Assailant, but Her Bones Were Broken by the Terrible Beating.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal. LAWRENCEBURG Ind.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 23.—The numerous posses which, day and night, have been scouring the country around Manchester Station in search of Rosa Kaiser, who was brutally assaulted, murdered and thrown into Tanner's creek Wednesday evening by an unknown negro who had previously beaten into insensibility and left for dead her father, seventy-three-year-old Martin Kaiser, were rewarded about 6 o'clock this morning by the finding of the girl's body in West Fork, a tributary of Tanner's creek, nearly three miles from the supposed scene of the tragedy.

The body, which lay close to the shore in a partly submerged clump of willows, was discovered by Leroy Clemm, a young man employed to look after the Big Four track lights along West Fork. All of the body save one hand was submerged, and it was this white hand on the surface of the water that attracted Clemm's attention.

Miss Kaiser evidently had been subjected to the most brutal and inhuman treatment. Her body was almost nude and bore unmistakable signs of the ravisher's work. The left arm was broken in two places and dislocated at the shoulder. There was a deep gash in her throat and her face was battered almost beyond recognition.

It was ascertained that the negro had kept his victim for some hours in a dismantled church about fifty yards from the junction of the West Fork and Tanner's creek. The interior of the church showed many indications of a terrible life-and-death struggle. There were numerous blood clots on the floor and walls. A blood-stained undergarment, identified as belonging to the murdered girl, was found near the crumbling altar.

The remains were taken to Guilford, Ind., on a handcar by section men and placed in the church to await the arrival of Coroner Swales, who was telegraphed for at once. Relatives arrived a few hours later and took charge of the body.

Martin Kaiser, father of the murdered girl, who came so near sharing, in a measure, her horrible fate, is expected to die at any moment. Mrs. Kaiser, who is confined to her bed with dropsy, suffered so severely from the effects of the shock that her life is despaired of.

Great excitement prevails in and about Manchester Station and the neighboring hamlets and a lynching or burning at the stake can scarcely be avoided if a suspect is captured and identified as the murderer in that locality. This morning this excitement assumed such a threatening aspect that it was deemed necessary to bring to this city for protection Louis Evenson, a negro suspect arrested at Cleves, O., last night and held there for identification. Accordingly, he was brought here about noon by Sheriff Axley and Marshal Jesse Crim, of Cleves, and placed in the county jail. Mrs. Mary Griffin and Mrs. Jane Darling, the two women who claim to have seen and talked with the supposed murderer a short time before the deed was committed, are expected to arrive here early to-morrow morning and identify Everson as the man who acted so suspiciously at their homes Wednesday afternoon. Everson is an exconvict. He is wanted at his home town, Rising Sun, Ind., for cutting with intent to kill. He is much feared in localities where he is well known.

When interviewed in his cell at the county jail this evening by a representative of the Journal, Everson admitted having passed through Manchester Station on the day of the murder, but emphatically denies any connection with the assault on either Mr. Kaiser or his daughter. Ever since his incarceration men from the remote country districts have been pouring into town and it is feared that a desperate effort will be made to lynch the negro. Sheriff Axley has placed a triple guard about the jail and every effort will be made to protect the prisoner from mob violence.

A post-mortem on the body of Rosa Kaiser develops the fact that she was not assaulted by her negro slayer, as was first supposed, evidently having perished in defense of her honor. Coroner Swaler, at the inquest this afternoon, rendered a verdict of "Murdered at the hands of some person or persons unknown, but believed to have been two negroes seen acting suspiciously near the scene of the crime shortly before the double assault was committed."

ANOTHER NEGRO WANTED
ATTEMPTED CRIMINAL ASSAULTS REPORTED IN DEARBORN.
The Perpetrator Escapes—Day of Excitement in and Around Lawrenceburg—Jail Heavily Guarded.
Associated Press Dispatch. LAWRENCEBURG.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 24.—This has been a day of intense agitation in the county over the murder of Rosa Kaiser and the murderous assault of her father last Wednesday night. Farmers gathered here, at Guilford, at Manchester and other towns in this county and openly threatened lynching if the guilty person could be identified. Sheriff Axby has a very strong guard of deputies at the jail to-night, where Louis Everson, known as "Black Ponto," is held on suspicion. There is no doubt that this negro would have been lynched to-day but for the announcement that Albert Darling, who came here from Manchester, did not identify him as the negro who called at the home of Mrs. Mary Griffin shortly before the assault on the Kaisers, and none of the other neighbors could identify the prisoner.

While the crowds were coming into town a dispatch was received that another outrage had been committed in the county and this diverted attention from the jail. Sheriff Axby, with deputies, was called to Weisburg, where an unknown negro, supposed to belong to the same railway construction gang, had criminally assaulted two little daughters of George Smith, a farmer. The sheriff was joined by many farmers in this chase and also by M. C. Cowdry, with his bloodhounds. After a hard chase it was found that the negro had boarded a freight train in the afternoon on the Big Four Railway at Sunman station, and when telegrams were sent after the train the negro could not be found. It is supposed he jumped off the train, possibly before it reached the next station, but he was on the cars long enough for the hounds to lose the trail.

Sheriff Axby, Deputy Patches and others returned to the jail here to-night, but the farmers, with the hounds, are still scouring the country. Sheriff Axby has a theory that the negro who escaped from Weisburg to-day is the one who assaulted the Kaiser family.

Mrs. Smith says she and her two little girls were alone in the house when the negro entered with a club. They screamed and escaped from the house and the negro fled in great haste before the neighbors reached them. Mrs. Smith's husband was taken to the asylum two weeks ago and it was known that she lived alone.

The funeral of Rosa Kaiser at Yorkville to-day was the most largely attended ever known in that vicinity and the feeling was intense. Neither of the parents could attend. The mother is a prostrated invalid and the father is still in a serious condition from his injuries.

John Frailor, of Seymour, was here tonight and identified the negro in jail as one who was in his meat store at Seymour the day following the Kaiser murder. The crowd had dispersed when this became known and all was quiet about the jail and in town, all the farmers being with the posses scouring the country for the Weisburg assailant. It was decided late tonight to take "Black Ponto" to Rising Sun for trial on an old charge of cutting to kill, and thus make sure of holding him, as it is believed that the prisoner is now at least implicated in the Kaiser tragedy.

CURE FOR LOCKJAW.

It is Discovered by Samuel Matthews Of Chicago.

Chicago, May 23.—It is announced at the University of Chicago that Dr. Samuel Matthews of Chicago has discovered a salt solution that will cure lockjaw, uraemia, locomotor ataxia and morphine poisoning. A solution of chlorite, sodium chloride, sodium sulphate, and sodium citrate is injected in large quantities into the patient's veins. The kidneys in particular are stimulated, and the entire nervous system is benefited.

The discovery of Dr. Matthews was made after he had experimented along the lines of the theories advanced by Profs. Jasquez Loeb and Albert P. Matthews, who held that the action of the 'inorganic suits on tissues of the body was electrical.

Practical appliances of Dr. Matthews' treatment at the university laboratories, it is said, have proved its success.

MACEDONIAN REVOLUTIONISTS

Turkish Troops Surround a Band And Destroy them.

Salwonica, May 24. The revolutionary band of 15 men, headed by the Macedonian leader, Svetkoff, against which the Turkish troops were fighting all day Thursday near the Bulgarian village of Nogil, six miles north of Monastir, was finally surrounded and destroyed. The fight was a prolonged one and Svetthoff, 12 of his men and six villagers, were killed. The Turkish loss was trifling. After the fighting the Bashl-Bazouks pillaged and burned 18 houses in Mogil.

Terror prevails in Monastir and the consuls propose to ask for foreign guards. Another 18 battalions of Turkish troops are coming from Asia Minor to complete the occupation of the villages.

Mob After a Negro.

Lawrence, Ind., May 24. A mob made up of farmers gathered here today and threatened to lynch Louis Everson, a negro held on suspicion of having murdered Rosa Kaiser and assaulted her father, on last Friday. The negro could not be identified, however.

During the excitement word was received that an unknown negro supposed to belong to the same construction gang, had assaulted two little daughters of George Smith, a farmer living in the country.

The mob, led by Sheriff Axyb, immediately started in search of this second negro, but after a hard chase it was found that he had escaped on a freight train.

Mrs. Smith states that she and her two little girls were alone in the house, when the negro entered with a club. They screamed and escaped from the house, when the negro fled. Mrs. Smith's husband was taken to the asylum two weeks ago, and she lives alone. Mobs are still searching.

Confessed His Crimes.

San Francisco, May 24.—Filled with remorse, J. T. Dent, alias S. W. Demison, who was recently arrested at Redding, has made a clean breast of his crimes at Americus, Ga., to which place he will be taken for trial. Requisition papers are now coming westward in the custody of Sheriff Bell of Sumter county, Georgia.

Dent managed to secure $15,000 from American citizens on various representations and on forged notes secured from banks sums aggregating $25,000. He then fled to California. He had opened a big music store at Americus with goods obtained from wholesale houses in other cities, sold the goods on credit and notes, duplicated and triplicated the notes and secured money from the banks upon the forged documents.

Heavy Rain in Nebraska.

Lincoln, Neb., May 24.—Another heavy rain tonight in southeastern Nebraska has added to the swollen condition of small streams, now out of their banks and flooding the farming country. In Oteo county eighty county bridges have been carried away by the high water, the damage being the greatest for twenty years.

King Edward's Health Good,

London, May 24—Lord Knollys, King Edward's private secretary, authorizes the Associated Press correspondent to say that there is absolutely no foundation for the report published in America that the king is in poor health. From many other sources closely associated with the court, it is learned that the king continues in the same good health which has enabled him to recently fulfil more public duties than he had ever before undertaken.

NEGRO SUSPECT IS FREED
NO EVIDENCE OF HIS COMPLICITY IN ROSA KAISER'S MURDER.
Stoned and Cursed by a Mob as He Leaves Lawrenceburg—Reward for Murderers of Sutton and Yeager.
pecial to the Indianapolis Journal.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 25.—Louis Everson, alias Black Ponto, the negro held here for identification as the murderer of Rosa Kaiser, was escorted down the Big Four tracks beyond the city limits this evening by Sheriff Axby and Officers Petcher and Justis and told to make himself scarce, an order which he lost no time in obeying. He was followed for fully a mile by a hooting mob of men and boys, who cursed, stoned and beat him. He finally escaped, and was last seen entering a strip of woodland, where he is supposed to have sought concealment.

Although no incriminating evidence could be secured against Everson, there are many persons who still believe him to be guilty, and it is probable that he will be sought out and tarred and feathered, if no worse fate is meted out to him, unless he makes good use of his liberty.

The release of Black Ponto was occasioned by the receipt of a telephone message from the mayor of Rising Sun to the effect that the warrant issued for him in that city several months ago, had been withdrawn. The mayor added that the further Everson remained from Ohio county the better it would be for his safety, as he probably would be mobbed should he venture to return there so intense is the feeling against him.

The search for the negro suspect seen in Seymour on Friday night proved fruitless, as did the search for the negro who tried to assault the Schmidt children at Weisburg yesterday. The search for alleged white accomplices has been abandoned.

A petition requesting the contractors in charge of the Big Four improvements between Lawrenceburg Junction and Sunman's to dispense with colored labor, is being circulated by Louis Kaiser, brother of the murdered girl. The presence of so many negroes is regarded as a menace to the community and unless the contractors heed the request embodied in the petition it is believed that a war of extermination will be inaugurated against the blacks by the incensed friends of the murdered girl.

Physicians in attendance on Mr. and Mrs. Kaiser report that the aged couple are improving slowly, but are not yet out of danger.

louis-everson-lawrenceburg-1903-05-24.A16:
MAY HAVE BEEN WHITE MAN.
New Theory Regarding the Kaiser Case at Lawrenceburg.
New Theory Regarding the Kaiser Case at Lawrenceburg.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 26.—While the sheriff and deputies and many farmers are still scouring the country for the murderer of Rosa Kaiser, it is now believed that the assault on both Rosa and her father was by a white man and not by a negro, and that revenge instead of robbery was the motive. Martin Kaiser and Frank Aust, an uncle of Rosa Kaiser, are both of this opinion. Aust said to-day: "The man who did the deed is closer at home than any negro."

It also develops that Barney Schimes, a decrepit white inmate of the infirmary, who had wandered away, is the one who so badly frightened the Smith girls on Sunday while their mother and brother were at church, and in their fright, they aroused the neighborhood by saying a negro assaulted them.

Late to-night it was learned that an arrest in connection with the murder of Rosa Kaiser would probably be made to-morrow. It was said that a relative is under suspicion of having committee the deed, but the name of the accused could not be learned to-night.

Louis Everson, alias Black Ponto, the negro suspect released from the county jail here yesterday and stoned out of town, was arrested by Detective Jack Loftus at Dillsboro early this morning and returned here about 10 o'clock. He was at once released by Sheriff Axby and left on the run for the line.
louis-everson-lawrenceburg-1903-05-24.A22:
MAKING WAR ON NEGROES.
Farmers in Dearborn County, Indiana, Avenging a Murder.

Farmers in Dearborn and adjoining counties of Indiana, are making a determined war upon negroes as a result of the murder of Miss Anna Kaiser.

Many families have been ordered to leave and negroes employed by farmers are being discharged.

Tuesday a committee of farmers, headed by Martin J. Kaiser, Jr., brother of the murdered girl, waited upon the superintendent of the Big Four construction work at Guilford and notified him that the negroes employed by him must leave.

louis-nicks-jeanerette-1903-08-25.A1:
KILLED BY A TOUGH.
Jeanerette, La.. August 25-Joseph Sanders, a merchant, was shot and killed by Louis Nicks, a negro tough. Nicks escaped, but a mob is in pursuit and a lynching will follow his capture. Nicks was engaged in a fight with another negro in Sanders' store, and when Sanders attempted to stop the row he was shot by Nicks.
louis-nicks-jeanerette-1903-08-25.A2:
Thirty Worthless Negroes Banished.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 26.--In consequence of the murder of a white man, Joseph Sanders, by a negro desperado named Louis Nicks, at Jeanerette, La., thirty negroes of that town who have been regarded as worthless were ordered by a committee of citizens to leave town and left at once. Nicks escaped after the murder and is hidden in a swamp.
louis-nicks-jeanerette-1903-08-25.A5:
Gold in Mexico. Mexico City, Aug. 26.—There is much excitement in the state of Oaxaca over the discovery of rich gold fields about 160 miles west of the city of Oaxaca and twelve miles from the town of Ejutla. The ore found assays up to $50,000 a ton, and so great is the local excitement that cavalry has gone to guard the claims located by enterprising and lucky miners. The ledge is said to be fifteen feet wide. Samples of the ore received here show it to be of a rich quality with threads of gold sticking out of the quartz. Negroes Ordered Out.
Jeanerette, La., Aug. 26.—As a result of the murder of Joseph A. Sanders, a merchant of this place, by Louis Nicks, a negro, several score of negroes were yesterday ordered to leave town immediately by the white people. Several of the negroes have left. Race feeling is running high and it would take very little to precipitate a bloody riot. A mob is pursuing Nicks and if he is captured he will never see the inside of a jail.

Stone at Austin.

Austin, Texas, Aug. 26.—City Attorney Stone of Houston was here yesterday conferring with the attorney general regarding a proposed bond issue for Houston amounting to $750,000, which will go toward public improvements. An issue of $100,000 will be presented and approved in advance of the others.

Child Fatally Burned.

Lake Charles, La., Aug. 26.—While playing with matches yesterday morning Bono, the 3-year-old son of Charles Gadman, a railroad man, received burns which will probably cause his death.

Child Died in Wandering.
Sonora, Texas, Aug. 26.—The little girl of Mr. M. C. Bozach, who was lost at Bond's ranch yesterday, has just been found on the ranch of S. L. Merch, some six miles from where it strayed. The child was dead when found.

Fifteen Acres to the Bale.
Franklin, Texas, Aug. 26.—The boll weevils are ruining crops here. Farmers estimate that it will take fifteen acres to make one bale. The rains caused their increase.

Babe Fell From Wagon.

Kaufman, Texas, Aug. 26.—Jim Meeks, who has just arrived from the Indian Territory, left his 17-months' old baby sleeping in the wagon, from which it fell, receiving injuries that resulted in almost instant death. They were at the home of his brother in North Kaufman, where they arrived yesterday morning.

Sour Lake, Texas, Aug. 26.—A mad gusher in the Cannon tract attracted considerable attention yesterday.
louis-nicks-jeanerette-1903-08-25.A6:
J. Sanders Murdered
At Jeanerette, this Parish, Sunday
The Murderer is Still at Large
Jaanerette, Aug. 24.—Joseph Sanders, the white man who was shot last night by Louis Nix, the negro barber who lives near the Southern Pacific depot, died at his residence today at 12:30 o'clock. Sheriff Henderson and deputies have been in pursuit of the negro since early this morning, but up to a late hour this evening he was still at large. Louis Nix, alias Tilou, is about forty years old, height five feet ten inches, weight 190 pounds, of brown color and wears a heavy black moustache. His clean-shaven face is covered with bumps. From reliable information received, it seems that the two men had quarreled, and Sanders struck Nix with a stick, whereupon the negro drew a revolver and shot him twice. Either wound would have proven fatal. Mr. Sanders leaves a wife and an adopted daughter, Mrs. W. D. Huff of Lafayette, who arrived here to-day with her husband. Mr. Sanders was well liked by the people here. The funeral will take place to-morrow from the Catholic church at Patoutville, La.—Special in T. D.
louis-nicks-jeanerette-1903-08-25.A7: Jeanerette, La., Aug. 25. About twenty-five or thirty negroes have been notified to leave town, and most of them did not wait for a second invitation. They are warned never to return. Although the excitement is intense, order and quiet prevails: but the feeling against the worthless class of negroes who have of late years infested this section is such that it would take very little to precipitate a bloody riot. If it does start, there is no telling where it will end. It Louis Nick is caught he will never see the inside of a jail. Joseph Amede Sanders, who died yesterday, at his residence, in this city, the victim of the negro, Louis Nicks, was buried to-day in the family cemetery at Patoutville. His funeral was largely attended. Louis Nicks, the murderer of Joseph Sanders, is still at large, and, although several arrests were made each time it proved to be the wrong party. Last night the negro section of the town was thoroughly searched, and al: though angry mutterings were heard on all sides, crowd was orderly and quiet. Not a negro loafer or "re-under," as they are called, was seen on the streets to-day. Nicks is well acquainted with the swamps, and it
louis-nicks-jeanerette-1903-08-25.A8:
is supposed that he made his way to Morgan City and is now in the swamps across Grand Lake. The hunt will be continued and if caught, summary punishment will be meted out to him.—Picaynne.

Franklin, La., Aug. 25.—Louis Nicks, the negro, who murdered Joseph Sanders at Jeanerette, Sunday night, came to Baldwin yesterday and went to Cypremont Swamp in this Parish, where his numerous relatives are living. The Sheriff and several Deputies were at the station here to arrest Nicks, but he got off at Baldwin, four miles west of Franklin. He is armed with the forty-five calibre Colt pistol with which he killed Sanders, and a good stock of ammunition, and the Duputies who are out to arrest him are anticipating a lively time. Picayune.
louis-nicks-jeanerette-1903-08-25.A9: Louis Nicks, the negro murderer has been captured and is now confined in the parish prison at this place awaiting trial. He was arrested at Baldwin, and was brought here in charge of Sheriff George Henderson on the 4:28 train on Wednesday afternoon.

LOCAL NEWS.
LOCAL NEWS.

The present week has been quite showery, but as the temperature has been high the two combined have produced ideal growing conditions for our cane planters, consequently sugar cane is growing rapidly, and numerous fine canes are brought out in evidence, if the present favorable weather keeps up we shall have a big cane crop. Cotton so far as heard from, is doing well the plant being large, well fruited, and no "boll weevils" or worms to bother us yet. Corn is considered made some is already gathered. This is a banner year. Rice harvesting was pretty general this week, although the many showers greatly retarded the work and had a tendency to discourage or the planters, but hot suns, nd clear skies soon evaporate the moisture and they are up and at it again. The quality of rice is fine and the yield promises to be handsome if only the prices can be maintained, then will our rice planters be on "easy street." We hear no complaint as regards labor.

Bargains in carpets, mattings and furniture six days in each week.—R. S. McMahon.

A most deplorable and painful accident occurred in the Enterprise printing rooms last Thursday afternoon, when Master Joel Fisher, brother of the editor was badly mutilated in the right hand from knuckles down. He was operating one of the power presses on a job of work, which becoming disarranged he attempted to rearrange while the press was in motion, when his hand was caught with above results. Drs. Rand and Sanders were called at once, who examined the hand and pronounced the bones broken, in fact badly crushed. Under their skillful treatment all will be done that can be done to restore the great damage. Joel although enduring excruciating pain, bore it with patience and fortitude. At this writing he is resting quietly.

Ostermoor Mattresses all sizes. Wernicke Elastic Book Cases.—R. S. McMahon.

Mr. and Mrs. J. G. Broussard, by the unscrutable act of Providence have been deprived of their little "Blanche," who died last Tuesday morning, aged 2 years and 5 months. While it is hard for us to submit to the decrees of providence, yet we must try to consider that "He doeth all things well," and the lovely bud He planted here, was needed to bloom in paradise forever, where parents may again rejoice in the companionship of their loved one. To such, their sorrow is not without hope. The funeral services were from St. Peter's church, Wednesday at 10 A. M.

China closets, glass ends from $10 up.—R. S. McMahon.

We were presented by Mr. A. E. Chastant last week, with a fine specimen of the cane crop of Mr. Anatole Judice, near Loreauville, this parish. His crop is very forward and uniform. The cane in question has over 5 feet of red joints of large diameter and lengths showing good culture hence rapid growth. Mr. Judice is one of the most successful in that very fertile section.

louis-nicks-jeanerette-1903-08-25.A11: Louis Nix, the negro who last Sunday night, shot and killed Joe Sanders, a white man, at Jeanerette, was arrested Wednesday morning at Baldwin by Deputy Sheriffs Alfred Pecot and Dudley Sanders. Nix admitted the killing, but declared the shooting had occurred in a general fight, in which he was knocked on the head and dazed. mooney-allen-beaumont-1903-07-23.A1:
NEGRO SHOT DOWN BY MOB
He Had Fatally Wounded Police man and Fired on Sheriff.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]
ston. Tex. July 23 - Mooney. Alle

Houston, Tex., July 23.—Mooney Allen, colored, was shot to death in the streets of Beaumont to-day by a pursuing mob of hundreds. More than a hundred shots were fired, and he was hit a dozen times. The chase was through the principal streets of the city.

Allen was notoriously bad. In the morning, after shooting at a colored policeman, who fled, he mortally wounded Policeman Stanbury, white, and took to the woods. Sheriff Landry and a posse followed him. He was captured and brought to the city in a hack. When in front of the telegraph office it was discovered that he was still armed. The Sheriff attempted to search him, and Allen fired his pistol at the officer, Landry returning the fire.

The negro jumped from the carriage and fled down the principal street, with a crowd in hot pursuit. He was fired at many times, but apparently without effect. Suddenly he turned and raised his revolver to shoot into the crowd. He faced a hundred guns and dropped with his body full of lead.
mooney-allen-beaumont-1903-07-23.A3:
NEGRO SHOT TO DEATH
KILLED A BEAUMONT POLICEMAN AND WAS PURSUED BY A MOB,
Which Kept Up a Constant Firing Until the Fugitive Fell Dead in the Street.
BEAUMONT, Tex., July 23.—Policeman Walter Skensbury was this afternoon shot and fatally wounded by Mooney Allen, a negro, who was pursued by a crowd of citizens and shot to death soon afterwards.

Allen started in to-day to shoot his wife and he forced a negro policeman and others who interfered to retreat. Skensbury appeared, when the negro covered him with a Winchester and told him to halt. The officer was surprised and did so, whereupon Allen fired, the bullet striking Skensbury in the side, passing through the body.

After firing the negro started down the street in the direction of the Thread-Needle House. Sheriff Landry's gun was empty, but at that instant some one placed a loaded revolver in his hands and he started after the negro. In the meantime a crowd of men, many of whom had pistols, started in pursuit of the negro. Some of them kept up a constant firing. The fugitive ran until he reached Cedar street. Here he turned, falling dead half way between Pearl and Main streets.
mooney-allen-beaumont-1903-07-23.A15:
NEGRO SHOOTS OFFICER.
Former Is Pursued by Many Persons and Shot to Death.
Beaumont, Tex., July 24.—Policeman Walter Skensbury was Thursday afternoon shot and fatally wounded by Mooney Allen, a negro, who was pursued by a crowd of citizens and shot to death shortly afterward. Allen started to shoot his wife, and he forced a negro policeman and others who interfered to retreat. Skensbury appeared, when the negro covered him with a Winchester and told him to halt. The officer was surprised, and did so, whereupon Allen fired, the bullet striking Skensbury in the side, passing through the body. After firing, the negro started down the street in the direction of the Threadneedle House. Sheriff Landry's gun was empty, but at that instant some one placed a loaded revolver in his hands and he struck out after the negro. In the meantime a crowd of men, many of whom had pistols, started in pursuit of the negro. Some of them kept up a constant firing and the fugitive kept running until he reached Cedar street. Here he turned and ran down Cedar street. He fell dead half way between Pearl and Main streets.

GENERAL NEWS.
per cent in 10 years.

— A negro mob lynched a negro tramp in Florida for assaulting a negro woman.

— The United States uses nearly a third more coffee than the rest of the world put together.

— About $100,000,000 worth of candy and confectionery are manufactured and sold in this country each year.

— Ten deaths from lookjaw have resulted in Cleveland, Ohio, since July 4th as a result of accidents with toy pistols.

— Dora Wright, colored, was hanged at South McAlister, I. T., on Friday for murder—beating a seven-year-old child to death.

— The executive office of the United States calls for only $112,000 a year, while England gives the royal family $4,000,000.

— The twelve-year-old son of J. D. Stevens, of Augusta, died of lookjaw, the result of a slight wound in the foot with a splinter.

— The first bale of new cotton from Zapata county, Texas, was sold on the New York cotton exchange on Tuesday, 21st inst., for 264 cents.

— The Kansas wheat crop is so large that a car famine exists. It is stated that the railroads do not own enough cars to handle the crop.

— A tornado killed five persons and injured a score of others at Streator, Ill. The same tornado killed four persons at Mendola, Ill.

— The First Baptist church. Wilmington, N. C., has resolved to discipline any of its members that may sign petitions for liquor license.

— The Georgia legislature killed the bill providing that convicts be required to work on the roads of the county in which they were sentenced.

— Twenty clerks of the New York Central railroad have been arrested for robbing freight cars. The populations amount to many thousand dollars.

— One hundred and fifty American teachers were at work in the schools of Porto Rico last year and are just now returning for their summer vacation.

— A negro man in Beaumont, Texas, in endeavoring to kill his wife, shot a policeman who attempted to arrest him. The man was promptly lynched.

— Gen. Cassius M. Clay died at his home in Lexington, Ky., on Wednesday at the age of 95. Gen. Clay was minister to Russia under Lincoln's administration.

— The troops have finally been withdrawn from Richmond and it is estimated that it has cost the State $50,000 to maintain peace during the street car strike.

— Notwithstanding the fact that polygamy is prohibited, the supreme court of Utah has ruled that a man is legally obligated to support his plural wives and educate his children by such unions.

Jim Gordon, who killed his brother and ran off with his widow, were lynched by a mob at Basin, Wyoming. In taking the men from jail the mob shot and killed Deputy Sheriff Pierce.

The rioting in Chicago is assuming more serious proportions. The mayor has issued a proclamation urging the people to keep away from the trouble and calling on the rioters to cease their work.

Citizens or Tioga, Pa., have erected a monument to the memory of John Schaffer, a railroad watchman, who was killed recently while attempting to save the life of a woman who was crossing the Reading tracks.

Mrs. Harriet Lane Johnston, who died recently, left $100,000 in her will for a monument to be erected at Mercersburg, Pa., to the memory of her uncle, James Buchanan, during whose administration as president she was mistress of the White House.

A sensation was created at Bloomington, Ill., by the arrest of Maude Jordine, seventeen years old, charged with the murder of her two-year-old sister Mabel. The baby was found hidden in some bushes near the Jordine home, most horribly mutilated.

Gov. Jeff Davis and Supreme Court Judge Davis are making a joint canvass of Arkansas for the office of governor. They became involved in a heated controversy at Hampton on Monday night and came to blows, but no damage was done and they made friends.

The defalcation of a confidential clerk in one of Buffalo's wealthiest law firms has been unearthed. The amount of the defalcation now aggregates about $800,000. None of the money was squandered, but was invested by the clerk in legitimate business enterprises in the name of "an Eastern capitalist."

It is reported that W. W. Hasslip, the Philadelphia treasure seeker, has found gold and silver which was buried on Warren island off Georgetown.

score injured by a tornado which swept over Streator and Mendota, Ill.

The battleship King Edward VII, the largest in the world, was launched at Davenport by the Princess of Wales last week.

Mooney Allen, colored, who shot and killed Policeman Spensbery at Beaumont, Tex., was riddled with bullets by a posse of citizens.

Isaac Ford, a negro confined in jail at Fort Worth on a charge of criminal assault, suicided by hanging himself with a rope made of a blanket.

Two non-union iron workers employed on a building at the St. Louis world's fair site, were badly injured in a riot started by union workmen.

Striking street car men or their sympathizers at Richmond used dynamite to blow up two cars operated by non-union men, and one was badly injured.

Editors J. M. Shepherd of the Warrenburg (Mo.) Standard-Herald, was fined $500 for contempt of the supreme court of Missour in criticising a ruling of that body. When the citizens of Warrensburg heard of the court's action the amount of the fine was at once raised by public subscription.

George Collins, who with another young man by the name of Rudolph robbed the Union, Mo., bank and later murdered Detective Schumacher, who was trying to effect their arrest, was convicted of murder in the first degree at Union, Mo., last week. Rudolph who escaped from the St. Louis jail a few weeks ago, is still at large.

Officers at St. Louis had a hard time to prevent the lynching of John Davis, colored, by members of his own race. Davis had just murdered his wife, and while the officers were awaiting the arrival of the patrol wagon a mob of 700 negroes made a rush to lynch the prisoner. The officers used their clubs and revolvers until reinforcements arrived.

General Cassius Marcellus Clay, ambassador to Russian under President Lincoln, noted abolitionist and author, died at his home, White Hall, Madison county, Kentucky, on the 22d. Death was due to general exhaustion. Gen. Clay was born October 19, 1810, in Madison county. He led a stirring life, which began to tell on him of late. He believed a conspiracy to assassinate him had been formed and some years ago fortified his home, White Hall, and entered a life of seclusion that ended only a few weeks ago when the courts appointed a committee to take charge of him and his effects.

The London Daily Mail's Tokie correspondent sends rather an alarming view of the situation in the east to his paper. He says that the increase of her fleet, the dispatch of reinforcements to Manchuria, the southward movement of the occupying army in Manchuria and the defiant conduct on the Korean frontier alarmed the Japanese, many of whom are convinced that it would be better to fight now than risk the eventual loss of Korea and the relegation of Japan to a secondary position. He says Japan is accumulating stores and negotiating for more ships; that a squadron is off Vladivostock, to which port Russian ships have been sent as a precaution, and that both fleets are ready for action. He says that a perusal of the Siberian press reveals the aggressive spirit of the Russian military party; that the Russians believe they will lose prestige if they give way now with the result that the far empire will be lost and Japanese influence will become predominant.

A strange condition of affairs exists in the town of Juana Diaz, in Porto Rico, all the merchants having colsed their places of business as a protest against paying excessive taxes.

A tornado five miles in width passed over a section of country near Marion, Ind. Everything in the storm's path was destroyed but fortunately no lives were lost. One farmer alone lost his entire corn crop, valued at $1,500.

At Patterson, N. J., three people were killed, one hundred injured and the streets strewn with debris by a tornado which struck that city. The property loss is placed at $200,000.

[Milwaukee Telegram to the St. Paul Pioneer Press.]

Miss Anna Evans, of this city, knows how to write a love letter. As a result of a competition carried on by a newspaper, she has received a $10 prize for having turned in the ideal love letter. It is as follows:

"MY DEAR HEART:—My first love letter! What shall I say to you? Why, that to-night I am rich—rich with a woman's whole opulence, the joy of giving.

"All my childhood's gladness, all of a girl's tender, secret dreaming of the unfolding mystery of life, all of a woman's yearning potentialities for sacrifice—all these I coin into the new, shining gold of my love, from mines whose depths are unguessed, unfathomed, save by you, and given not in spendthrift recklessness, but with jealous care, that every bit of its preciousness may come to you untouched.

"Yes, I'm jealous—not of you for me, but of my love, for you. Because, unspeakably dear as your love is to me that is my life, my love for you. I think that must be God's gift to woman, and even that I give to you. Good-night."

He Stabbed Chinaman, Mob Pursued Dragged from Cellar.
Oscar Franklin, a colored waiter, of No. 241 West Twenty-ninth-st., entered the chop suey restaurant of Loo Sung, at No. 331 Eighth-ave., last night, in a Tuxedo suit, with a colored woman, a merry mood and the price of one bowl of chop suey. He was served. Then he sang ragtime songs. Loo Sung did not appreciate his presence. When Franklin demanded an extra knife and fork Loo Sung refused to supply him. Moreover, he wanted the price of the contents of the bowl into which the woman was delving.

Franklin, it is alleged, handed him the bowl with more haste than courtesy. Other crockery sped about the room. Franklin and his companion started to leave. The Chinaman grabbed him. Franklin, it is said, stabbed the hand the Chinaman had laid on him. Loo Sung, with a police whistle, ran to a window.

Policeman Beattie, of the West Thirty-seventh-st. station, caught sight of Franklin, deserted by his companion, speeding through Twenty-seventh-st. toward Ninth-ave. The negro had a good start and turned Ninth-ave. twenty yards ahead. Down Ninth-ave. he ran, and then around Twenty-sixth-st. toward Eighth-ave. Beattie was still in pursuit. Passing Franklin Terrace, in Twenty-sixth-st., the negro looked over his shoulder and caught sight of a mob following the policeman. Then he darted in the terrace and crawled into the furthest corner of a cellar.

Beattie dragged him out, and was met by the mob, who yelled:

"Lynch him! String him up!"

Beattie drove back the mob. Two policemen arrived from adjacent posts and helped him take his prisoner to the station.

Jackson, Jan. 20.—The whitecap outrages in southern Mississippi have assumed the form of occasional echoes, and the disturbances are practically at an end. Between the whitecaps and the labor agents the result both set out to accomplish has been brought about, which naturally suggests that it is high time for both parties to quit operations.

The latest work of the whitecaps was the notification given the manager of the Cumberland Telephone-Company at Osyka and Magnolia to take all phones out of nergo houses. The manager declined to comply with the request and has offered a reward of $100 for the arrest of the parties who sent the notice.

The whitecaps burned the home of a nergo named Williams, living in the neighborhood of Johnston Station on Saturday night. Williams disregarded the notice to leave the community before the first of January.

In many of the communities the whitecappers have been thoroughly quelled by the mass meetings held by the law-abiding citizens, and the several arrests made have convinced them that the crusade is a determined one.

ENGINEER FOILED PLAN
(By Associated Press.)

HUNTINGTON, W. VA., July 31.—The Chesapeake and Ohio express train, No. 1. was held up by a mob of 200 men near Clifton Forge late last night, and a desperate effort was made to take two negro prisoners from the train. Over a hundred shots were fired by the mob, and when the train reached here twenty bullets were buried in the woodwork of the smoking car and all of the window glass had been shot out.

At Clifton Forge the two negro prisoners were taken on board to be brought to Covington Va., for safekeeping. Engineer James Peck, of Hinton, and Conductor Jack Hall, of this city, who were in charge of the train, saw lights waving on the track just as the train had begun to gather speed after leaving Clifton Forge. The train was stopped immediately, and Engineer Peck started to get out of his engine to find out why the train had been flagged. As the train came to a standstill a mob surrounded the engine and coaches, and threatened to shoot Engineer Peck if he moved the train. They began to climb aboard. Conductor Hall, who had anticipated trouble when he saw the train flagged, was prepared for the mob, and as they made a rush for the coaches ordered all the doors of the cars locked. The mell, finding that it would be impossible for them to enter and obtain the negroes, began to gather around the smoking car, in which the negroes were under guard.

OPENED FIRE.

As Conductor Hall ran through the train calling upon the passenger to lie flat on the floor, the mob began firing into the windows of the smoker, while the passengers scrambled from their seats to a place of safety from the flying bullets. The firing was kept up for several minutes, and bullets whistled through the car windows.

While women screamed, the mob outside continued their clamoring for the two negro prisoners. Revolvers were also brought into play, and flying missiles of all descriptions came through the windows, but not a passenger or trainman was injured.

Engineer Peck, during the firing, had sat upon his engine, covered by revolvers in the hands of several members of the mob. At last, when the main body of the mob had almost exhausted their supply of bullets, those who had been guarding the engineer, left, going towards the smoker, leaving Peck unguarded. As his former guards turned and ran toward the smoking car, Peck pulled the trottle wide open and the train began to move.

PARTING SHOTS.

The mob, seeing the turn things were taking, and fearing they might be outdone in their efforts to get the prisoners, climbed up on the platforms of the cars and attempted to stop the train by turning the angle cock to the air nose, thereby applying the brakes. Not understandong the working of the brakes, however, they were unable to apply them at full pressure, as the train had gotten under headway. Realizing that they were baffled, the men jumped from the moving train and fired several farewell shots into the car windows.

The train gained quick momentum, and did not stop until Covington was reached, where the negroes were placed in jail.

The negroes for which the train was held up are from Lynchburg, Va., and are supposed to be the men who shot and seriously injured Harry Rudisell on the Chesapeake and Ohio excursion between Clifton Forge and Lynchburg a few days ago. Rudisell is in the hospital in Clifton Forge in a critical condition.

CLIFTON FORGE, VA., August 1.—The Clifton Forge Rifles were called to Covington, Va., at 10:25 P. M. by Deputy Sheriff Sizer to aid the civil authorities to protect from a mob of four hundred or more men the two negro prisoners, Willie and Otho Green, who are in the Covington jail, for the shooting of Harry Rudisill, on an excursion train Wednesday night.

These men were taken to Covington on Thursday night by the authorities for safe-keeping till Rudisill became well enough to identify them.

A mob is assembling and threats of lynching are heard on every side. Reports were on the streets here to-day to the effect that a mob would lynch them to-night, and Captain Roberts, of the Rifles, was notified to hold his company in readiness. The negro prisoners are the ones who were aboard No. 1 on Thursday night, when an angry mob of two hundred men made an effort to secure them. Not succeeding, they fired several hundred shots at the train, knocking out the windows and otherwise injuring the cars. Harry Rudisill still lingers in a dangerous condition, recovery very doubtful.

Efforts to reach Covington failed, owing to the fact that the telegraph office was closed for the night.

Judge Anderson Tells Story of How Man at Covington Was Protected.
Judge George K. Anderson, of Alleghany, who presides over the County Court of that and several adjoining counties, and who, after February 1st next, will preside over the Circuit Court for the district of Alleghany, Bath, Highland and Botetourt, is in the city on legal business.

Speaking of the presence of the two negroes, William and Otho Green, who shot Harry Rudisile, a white man on a James River division train, in Clifton Forge, and of the subsequent developments in connection with the case, Judge Anderson said that the troops had been ordered to Covington to protect the negro and to deliver him safe at Lynchburg by the Sheriff who had authority to do so without calling on the Governor in an emergency such as that presented.

"The negroes committed the offense in Bedford county, were arrested on a train of the James River division of the Chesapeake and Ohio road by a special officer, and turned over to the sheriff of Rockbridge at Buena Vista. It seems that they were then taken from Lexington. Clifton Forge and carried to the Chesapeake and Ohio Hospital, where the wounded man was for identification. The man had just been operated on and was under the influence of chloroform and could hardly have identified any one. By what authority the bringing of the man from Lexington was done or by whose orders I do not know. This was done, however, and the negroes were afterwards started for Covington. The fast train No. 1 was flagged by a mob, and it was then that all of the windows of the car were shot out in the effort to get the negroes. The engineer coolly pulled out while the mob was interested in the shooting, and the negroes were thus landed in safety in Covington jail.

The military were sent from Clifton Forge to Covington Saturday night, and a telephone message was sent to Superintendent Carlisle, of the Chesapeake and Ohio road, to send a train to take the negroes to Lynchburg. At 2 o'clock the negroes and the troops were hurried aboard the train and the run begun. The train went through Clifton Forge at good speed, having a clear track and being shifted to the James River division track, continued its run without a stop. It was the first time for many years that a train has been through Clifton Forge without stopping, but it was the only awy to get those prisoners through in safety. ASSAILANTS ARE IN BEDFORD CO. JAIL Military Guard Prevented the Lynching of Willie and Otho Green. (Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
COVINGTON, VA., August 3.—Threats to lynch Willie and Otho Green, two negro men, who were in jail here, charged with shooting Harry Rudesill, caused Deputy Sheriff A. C. Sizer to place strong guard around jail and call on Clifton Forge Rifles for help Saturday night.

When reports were circulated here late Saturday evening that a mob from Clifton Forge would attempt to get the prisoners from jail, Deputy Sheriff Sizer at once began to make preparations to guard the jail. Fifteen or twenty men were summoned and supplied with arms. When it was learned that an armed guard had been stationed around the jail no little excitement prevailed, and the arrival of a mob from Clifton Forge was expected.

About 9 o'clock a message from Clifton Forge stated that a mob was being formed and was almost uncontrollable. Threats of lynching were constantly heard, and the men composing the mob seemed determined to get the prisoners. The guard around the jail was at once increased, many of the young men of Covington being summoned to assist in defending the prisoners and keeping order.

Mr. Sizer had called for the military at Clifton Forge. Between 11 o'clock and midnight Captain Roberts arrived with the Clifton Forge Rifles on a special train, and after stationing guards in different parts of the town placed most of his troops around the jail.

A short time before the troops arrived a fire broke out, and the ringing of the fire bell was thought by many people to be the announcement of the mob's arrival. The old hose-house, near the center of the town and about 400 yards from jail, was on fire in two places. This fire was soon put out, but there is a general belief that the building was set on fire by a representative of the mob, who desired to attract the attention from the jail.

All through the night strange men were seen walking the streets and often would form into small bands and hold long and animated conversations. There was no attempt made to force an entrance to the jail, although at several times a mob seemed to be forming. The night had grown intensely dark, and all effort to ascertain the movements of the strange men were mostly in vain.

Sheriff F. M. Turner arrived on No. 2 about 12 o'clock and decided to take the prisoner to Bedford City for safekeeping. As the shooting of Rudesill occurred in Bedford county, the prisoners properly belonged in Bedford jail. panted by the military, put the two negroes on a special train and started for Bedford City by way of Lynchburg. As soon as the soldiers left, taking the prisoners, the former quiet of the town prevailed. The citizens of Covington are unantmous in commending Deputy Sheriff Sizer for his firm stand and purpose to suppress all violence.

LYNCHBURG, VA., August 3.—A special train arrived yesterday about 10 o'clock over the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway, from Covington, having on board the Clifton Forge Rifles, consisting of forty-two men, under Captain Roberts, who were escorting to this city for safekeeping William and Otho Green, the negroes who are charged with shooting Harry Rudisill, of Eagle Mountain, on an excursion train at Abert station, eight miles west of here, last Wednesday night. The negroes were in charge of Sheriff Turner, of Alleghany county, and Deputy-Sheriff Hornsberger. With the company guarding them, the two negroes, handcuffed together, were marched to the jail where they were turned over to Jailer Frank Wellford.

One of the negroes is a light mulatto and the other quite dark. They stated that they were half brothers, eighteen and twenty-four years of age, respectively; were raised in Buchanan, but were working as farm laborers on Captain Echols' old place, at Balcony Falls. They did not express themselves as to their guilt or innocence, and did not seem frightened.

After placing them in jail Sheriff Turner communicated with Judge Brown, of Bedford, by 'phone, and the latter sent Sheriff Huddleston and a deputy here on No. 4, and they returned to Bedford City with the prisoners on the train, which leaves here at 5:50 P. M. As the offense was committed in Bedford county, the prisoners will be tried at Bedford City. When arrested, they were taken to Lexington, and on Thursday were conveyed to Clifton Forge, to be taken before Harry Rudisill, who was in hospital there, for identification. Rudisill's condition was so critical that they were then put on the fast passenger train for Covington, but only reached there after the train had been riddled with bullets by a mob.

Two Hundred Men, After Two Negroes, Fire Into Cars.

Fast express train No. 1 on the Chesapeake and Ohio, Washington to Cincinnati, was held up near Clifton Forge, Va., Friday night by 200 armed men, whose object was to take a couple of negro passengers from the train and lynch them. The attempt to get the men was unsuccessful.

The posse flagged the train with red lanterns, and when the engineer brought the train to a standstill he was covered with revolvers and told that if he attempted to move on he would be shot.

The conductor on hearing the mob outside quickly locked the door of the front coach, and as it was impossible for the frenzied men to enter, owing to the vestibulated platform, they became so enraged that they began firing into the front coach, which was occupied by the prisoners. Fully fifty shots were fired into the car, but the prisoners and the few passengers that were in this car lay on the floor and escaped uninjured. Almost every window in the coach was broken. When the fusillad of bullets began the men who were on the engine leaped off to participate, and Engineer Wise opened the throttle and pulled out. Strange to say, no one aboard the train was injured. The negroes had been arrested near Lexington, Va., charged with fatally shooting Will Rambow, a Chesapeake and Ohio brakeman, on the James River division of the road, and were being taken to Covington, Va., for safe-keeping.

The United States authorities have been notified of the hold-up of the train, which was a fast mail, and it is more than likely that an effort will be made to arrest all implicated.

INQUIRY INTO HOLD-UP

The Chesapeake and Ohio Railway has ordered every detective in its service together with half a dozen private detectives, to Clifton Forge, Va., to ascertain, if possible, the names of every one connected with the mob that held up one of their fastest express trains in that place Thursday night for the purpose of taking two negro passengers with a view of
selected with the mob that held up one of their fastest express trains in that place Thursday night for the purpose of taking two negro passengers with a view of lynching them.

The United States government also has sent detectives there, as the train held up contained a mail car, and this was punctured by a number of bullets.

Will and Otto Green, the two negroes who were in jail at Covington, Va., on the charge of shooting Harry Rudisill on an excursion train last Wednesday night, were brought here for safe keeping. The prisoners were taken to jail at Lexington first after having been arrested, and on Thursday night were taken to Clifton Forge for identification by Rudisill. He was not in condition to see them, however, and on Friday night they were taken to Covington.

The negroes were landed in Covington jail, but the excitement did not subside. SAVANNAH. GA.. SATURDAY. AUGUST 8. 1903.
MOBHELD UP TRAIN

USED MUCH AMMUNITION

The Chesapeake and Ohio express train No. 1 was held up by a mob of two hundred men near Clifton Forge, West Virginia, at a late hour Friday night and a desperate effort was made to take two negro prisoners from the train. Over a hundred shots were fired by the mob, and when the train reached Huntington 20 bullets were buried in the woodwork of the smoking car and all of the windows had been shot out.

At Clifton Forge the two negro prisoners were taken on board to be sent to Covington, Va., for safe keeping. Engineer James Peck, of Hinton, and Conductor Jack Hall, of Huntington, who were in charge of the train, saw lights waving on the track just as the train had begun to gather speed after leaving Clifton Forge. The train was stopped immediately, and Engineer Peck started to get out of his engine to find out why the train had been flagged.

As the train came to a standstill, a mob surrounded the engine and coaches, and threatened to shoot Engineer Peck if he moved the train. Then they began to climb aboard. Conductor Hall, who had anticipated trouble when he saw the train flagged, was prepared for the mob, and as they made a rush for the coaches, he ordered all the doors of the cars locked. The men, finding that it would be impossible for them to enter and obtain the negroes, began to gather around the smoking car, in which the negroes were under guard. As Conductor Hall ran through the train calling upon the passengers to lay flat on the floor, the mob, began firing into the windows of the smoker, while the passengers scrambled from their seats to a place of safety from the flying bullets. The firing was kept up for several minutes, and bullets whistled through the car windows. While women screamed, the mob outside continued their clamoring for the two negro prisoners. Flying missiles of all description came through the windows, but not a passenger or trainman was injured. Engineer Peck, during the firing, had sat upon his engine covered by revolvers in the hands of several members of the mob.

NEGRO'S HOUSE IS BURNED BY WHITES
During an Encounter the Negro Shot Two White Men
CROWD AFTER VENGEANCE
Shots Were Fired Before the House Was Burned In Hopes of Dislodging the Negro, But He and Friend Had Escaped.
Anniston, July 22.—(Special.)—H. Clay Davis of this city spent Saturday in Pell City and tells of an encounter that took place between some factory hands and a negro, which resulted in two white men being seriously shot by the negro. He said that the negro and white men had a quarrel at a baseball game that was being played between Ashville and Pell City at the place and that the negro was run out of the crowd by the men and pursued to his home, where he secured a Winchester rifle, and as the pursuers came up he fired upon them, wounding two white men, whose names could not be learned. He said that the negro's house was located about a mile from Pell City, on the road to Sedden, and that just before leaving the place Saturday night the house was in flames and was burned completely down by the friends of the two men that were shot.

Davis said that before firing the house the men fired a number of shots for the purpose of dislodging the negro, but he had fled with another negro before the arrival of the crowd, and that the party was in pursuit of the two when last heard of. It is thought that the negro evaded the crowd, as nothing of a lynching bee has been heard from Pell City, and this seemed to be the purpose of the mob.

Charles Rohnuer, the young white man convicted on a charge of burglary in the Police court yesterday morning, made an attempt to escape from the city jail yesterday afternoon. He had removed several bricks from the wall of his cell when his work was discovered. He had in some way secured a number of nails and a pine knot. The mortar was removed from between the bricks with a nail and the bricks loosened by striking them with the pine knot. They were then taken out, piled in a corner and covered with a blanket. A large hole had been made when discovered.

In a spirited race last night Mr. Thos. Collins of the Pipe Fitters' union was elected president of the trades council for the ensuing term. Other officers elected were: Vice president, W. A. Pilkington; recording secretary, Lee Ferguson; delegate to American Federation of Labor, Lee Ferguson; alternate, C. C. Echard.

The election for president was spirited and quite interesting, and it required the third ballot to elect.

ALSTON TELLS THE JURY OF A CRIME
Discusses Riot at Pell City in Vigorous Terms
ACTION OF MOB CENSURED
Judge Points Out That an Uncalled for Attack Was Made on Negro Home and Characterizes the Deed as Cowardly.
Pell City, July 23.—(Special.)—A special jury has been summoned by Judge A. H. Alston, supernumerary judge presiding over the Circuit court here for the purpose of investigating the lawlessness of last Saturday when a mob chased a negro and wounded him and burned down the home of an innocent negro who had nothing to do with the disturbance. In instructing the jury Judge Alston handled the subject in a vigorous manner, and spoke of the disorders in unvarnished terms. His charge was as follows:

The Charge.

You are doubtless surprised to be called upon to serve your county in your present capacity so soon after the adjournment of the regular grand jury that was organized in this court room on last Monday. It having been brought to my attention that an indictable offense has been committed in the southern judicial division of this county during the session of this court, but after the adjournment of the grand jury, and the offense being such a heinous one, I decided it was my duty to this county and to the state to exercise the authority conferred by statute on circuit judges in matters of this extraordinary nature, hence I have ordered a special grand jury summoned from the qualified citizens of this county, in order that an immediate investigation may be had and the guilty party or parties brought to justice. The report that has been brought to me is this: On last Saturday afternoon at the ball grounds near here there was a negro man, known as being "goosey;" he was "goosed" by some young white men, and at the time he had in his hands a rock, which he threw down, and it struck one of the young white men, who became angry. The negro ran away and was pursued by a crowd of thirty or more white men. The sheriff was present and urged the parties to desist, but his remonstractions were met with oaths and the crowd continued to pursue the negro and were threatening to do violence to him, several of them being drunk.

Defense of a Home.

The negro finally reached his home and there secured his rifle, and warned the crowd not to advance upon him; but they did advance and fired upon him; he returned the fire and wounded two of the crowd. His house was fired into and a child wounded and the pursued negro was also slightly wounded. The negro escaped. About 10 o'clock that night the mob returned, but failing to find the negro, they then set fire to an adjacent dwelling occupied by a family of negroes in no way connected with the man to visit lawless violence. And today there is a family homeless and without food or clothing, all they possessed having been destroyed by the flames started by a lawless mob. It is true, gentlemen of the grand jury, that family is composed of humble negroes, but I trust I am addressing sixteen men whose sense of justice as well as moral and physical courage are too high to allow them to consider for a moment the condition in life of any man or set of men, in the discharge of the responsible duties now devolving upon you.

We often hear it said that a negro must keep in his place. I thoroughly agree with such sentiment. It is a part of my nature, acquired by inheritance as well as education. And I say the white man should also keep in his place. The place of the white man is by the God that made him one of superiority, and it should be maintained and not be lowered of undue familiarity. If a white man is upon a footing with the negro, he ought not to want to mob him, if a falling out results from that undue familiarity.

Negroes Are Dependent.

Gentlemen of the jury, no people on earth are so dependent as are the negroes upon the whites for justice. They have been disfranchised by us, and, in my judgment, most properly and wisely. They have no voice in the selection of those who make the laws that govern them. Nor do they sit upon juries or exercise any other rights of citizenship. They are helpless and absolutely dependent upon us for their equal rights and protection. Our responsibility is as great as their dependence upon us. But I am sure we are equal to it and that the great majority of the white people in Alabama desire to see the negro undisturbed in the enjoyment of every right that the law gives him. Let him feel that he will be justly dealt with; that his liberty and his property are as secure and as safely guarded by the laws of Alabama as are the white man's. The theory of our law is equal protection to all of its citizens. It rests evenly upon the humble and the exalted, and upon the poor and the rich, the black and the white. And it will be a sad day in Alabama when we depart from that theory of the law.

Guilty Should Be Punished.

The guilty should be punished and the innocent acquitted, regardless of color or

Guilty Should Be Punished.
The guilty should be punished and the innocent acquitted, regardless of color or condition of life. That man who possesses that high order of courage that is God-given and which we all admire never opposes or deprives the weak of any right; but, upon the other hand, his voice and heart are always raised in behalf of truth and justice.

Gentlemen of the grand jury, you are confronted by an indisputable fact and it is this: In a short distance from the court house there can be found a heap of ashes that represent a destroyed home by the hand of a lawless and violent mob. And it is for you to ascertain, if by diligent inquiry you can, who committed this cruel and cowardly crime. Any person who maliciously and intentionally burns a dwelling house, whether there is in it at the time of such burning any human being or not, is guilty of arson in the first degree, and must on conviction be punished at the discretion of the jury by death or imprisonment in the penitentiary for not less than ten years.

Crime Confronts the Jury.

I have said to you that the commission of this outrageous crime confronts you, and I have informed you what constitutes the crime as well as the punishment, for it is fixed by law. But this court is powerless to administer the law by placing the guilty man upon trial until a true bill has been duly returned into this court by a legally constituted grand jury. Gentlemen, it would be hard to imagine a more dangerous citizen than he who for any cause would, under the cover of darkness, apply the torch to the home of another to gratify malice. Such a cowardly creature would not hesitate to plunge the deadly dagger into your heart or assassinate you while asleep.
